News.title: Murder probe launched after dad, 56, killed in ‘violent’ village street brawl
News.content:
Murder probe launched after dad, 56, killed in ‘violent’ village street brawl

Anthony Jones, known as Tony, 56, from Brecon, died in hospital after sustaining life-threatening injuries during violent disorder in Wales on Thursday evening.

View 2 Images Anthony "Tony" Jones, 56, has died following the disorder (Image: Gwent Police)

A murder inquiry has been launched, and seven men have been arrested by police after a 56-year-old died.

‌



Following a violent disturbance near Pontypool, Wales, on Thursday evening, three men were taken to hospital, with two of those initially said to be in a critical condition.

‌



Gwent Police has confirmed one has since died after sustaining life-threatening injuries.

‌



Officers were called to reports of "violent disorder" involving a group of men in Mill Street, at around 7.15pm on Thursday, August 6.

Anthony Jones, known as Tony, 56, from Brecon, passed away in hospital. His family are being supported by specialist officers.

In total, seven men – aged 31, 39, 40, 45, 59, 61, and 73 - have been arrested in connection with the disorder. All seven remain in police custody.

‌



Senior investigating officer, Detective Superintendent Laura Bartley said: "We recognize that reports of this nature will cause concern in our community, but we have officers working around the clock conducting inquiries as part of the investigation.

View 2 Images Forensic officers at the scene of the incident on Friday morning (Image: John Myers)

"We're trying to establish the movements of those involved both before and after the disorder and are asking motorists who were driving along Hospital Road, Mill Road and the surrounding areas between 6pm and 9pm on Thursday to check their dashcam footage.

Article continues below

"Anyone with any information is urged to submit information via the Major Incident Public Portal or contact us quoting log reference 2600255536."

Those with any information are urged to call 101, visit the Gwent Police website or send a direct message via social media. Alternatively, Crimestoppers can be contacted anonymously by calling 0800 555 111 or through their website.

On Friday morning, a police cordon remained in place at Mill Road and Hospital Road as investigations into the incident continued. Forensics officers were active at the scene, placing evidence markers on the ground outside Pontnewynydd sports and social club.

News.title: UFO files claim 'dead spaceman' found inside mysterious metal sphere after it crashed to Earth
News.content:
UFO files claim 'dead spaceman' found inside mysterious metal sphere after it crashed to Earth

US government officials launched an investigation into bizarre claims that a 'dead spaceman' was found inside a metal sphere that fell to Earth in Brazil, the latest UFO files reveal

View 3 Images An artist's impression of the UFO orb (Image: UFOdailysightings/YOUTUBE)

An investigation was launched into bizarre claims that a UFO crashed to Earth with the body of a dead spaceman inside, newly declassified US government files reveal.

‌



The UFO hunt was launched after officials picked up on a local radio broadcast in Conde, Brazil, on November 8, 1963, which reported that a large metal sphere had fallen to the ground, leaving a large crater in the centre of the town. It was said to contain a human body wearing a uniform, and had inscriptions that 'could not be deciphered'.

‌



Details of the alleged incident were quickly circulated across Brazilian media, catching the attention of the US State Department, the Department of Defence, and NASA.

‌



View 3 Images A US Department of Defence telegram about the 1963 incident is included in the latest release of UFO files (Image: US Department of War)

On November 14, 1963 - six days after the initial radio broadcast - the US Embassy in Rio de Janeiro sent a telegram to the State Department and the American Consulate in Salvador asking for clarification. But five minutes later, the embassy clarified that no craft had actually been recovered from the ground.

A final diplomatic cable dated November 20 revealed the entire episode appeared to have been fabricated in Rio de Janeiro. Journalists and investigators had travelled to Conde, but failed to find a single person who had witnessed an unusual object falling from the sky.

‌



It read: "Story of strange object descending in region of Conde Bahia apparently fabricated in Rio no such objects seen by anyone in the area according to newspaper reporters and others who rushed there before investigation reports were received. Secretary Public Security speculated object might be weather balloon - but no such sighting verified."

View 3 Images The Pentagon has released the latest batch of UFO files (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The 1960s telegram is included in the latest batch of 'UFO files' released by the Pentagon. It follows the launch of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE) earlier this year, which seek to declassify government files related to Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) and UFOs.

Article continues below

Among the 41 documents featured in the latest release is a US Navy Photographic Interpretation Centre review of alleged UFO footage captured in Montana and Utah, which was found to be "inconsistent with those of natural phenomena or commonly known aerospace technologies."

Another file details a September 2021 encounter by Special Operations forces aboard an AC-130J gunship, where the crew observed 25 "cold orbs" flying at speeds between 250 and 1,300mph. The orbs were said to have performed aggressive manoeuvres, and appeared to react to the aircraft's cannon fire.

An FBI interview record meanwhile details a recent eyewitness account in which "multiple red lights" and orb-like objects were seen moving above a mountain ridge in the western US.

News.title: Andy Burnham promises crackdown on costly subscription traps and 'rip-off discounts'
News.content:
Andy Burnham promises crackdown on costly subscription traps and 'rip-off discounts'

The Prime Minister will bring forward 'easy to exit' rules, making it less painful for consumers to cancel subscriptions and avoid automatic renewal at a higher cost

View 2 Images Andy Burnham will bring forward 'easy to exit' rules (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Andy Burnham has promised everyday fixes on the cost of living including an end to costly subscription traps and rip-off discounts.

‌



The Prime Minister will bring forward “easy to exit” rules, making it less painful for consumers to cancel subscriptions and avoid automatic renewals at a higher cost. The crackdown was previously unveiled under ex-PM Keir Starmer and is set to include mandatory reminders before renewals of 12-month contracts.

‌



The rules had been due to come into force in Spring 2027, but Mr Burnham will now bring forward by several months to January in time for when customers often start new subscriptions. Downing Street has said it will save consumers an estimated £400 million - or £14 each month per unwanted subscription.

‌



Andy Burnham kicks off summer tour of UK to hear from voters on cost of living READ MORE :

Voters say mental health support over benefit cuts is best way to get young back into work READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has said his government wants to put more money in people's pockets (Image: Getty Images)

No10 also said “pretend prices and deceptive deals will be a thing of the past” under new proposals. They said the Prime Minister plans to ban retailers from making misleading claims to customers about discounts after complaints prices are being artificially hiked to give a false sense of value.

Mr Burnham said: “I know people are sick and tired of rip-off discounts and subscription traps. Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles like this are just part of life.

‌



“I don’t think that’s right, especially when the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on so many people’s lives. I’m determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living.”

He added: “We’re putting an end to phoney bargains. If something is advertised as half price, it should actually be half price. We’re also making it as easy to leave a subscription as it is to join.

“These are just two of the everyday fixes we’re going to be rolling out – today is just the start. We want to put more money in people’s pockets and give people hope that politics really can work for them and their everyday lives.”

Article continues below

Chief executive of Citizens Advice, Dame Clare Moriarty, said: “For too long consumers have been tricked into paying for products or services they don’t use - or didn’t even want to begin with - costing millions of pounds each year. So we really welcome the government’s move to speed up action on subscription traps and look at banning other tactics firms use to catch consumers out.”

She added: “At Citizens Advice, we’ve sounded the alarm on this for years, because we know subscription traps and sneaky online practices that hit consumers’ pockets hard are a widespread problem. We previously found that over 13 million people (26% of UK adults) accidentally took out a subscription in a year.”

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds added: “There’s nothing worse than realising you’ve been fleeced by a dodgy deal, or seen money leaving your account because of a subscription you didn’t want to renew or couldn’t easily cancel. This Government is on the side of families working hard to make ends meet, while making sure the rules are clear for businesses and easy to follow.”

News.title: Andy Burnham kicks off summer tour of UK to hear from voters on cost of living
News.content:
Andy Burnham kicks off summer tour of UK to hear from voters on cost of living

EXCLUSIVE: Prime Minister Andy Burnham tells The Mirror he'll be spending the month 'out of Westminster and into your town' to ask people 'what would actually make your life better?'

View 3 Images PM Andy Burnham is expected to spend the rest of the summer on the road (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham is set to kickstart a summer tour of the country this week and ask voters directly: "What would actually make your life better?"

‌



The new Prime Minister, who returns from a short holiday abroad this week, is expected to spend the rest of August on the road visiting every nation and region across Britain. In the coming days he is also set to outline measures to tackle misleading discounts and rip-off prices while promising action to get high streets thriving again.

‌



Mr Burnham told The Mirror: “This month I'm out of Westminster and into your town. Not for the photographs, but because I want to hear directly from people in their communities. I'll be asking one question: what would actually make your life better?

‌



View 3 Images Andy Burnham reintroduced the £2 cap on bus fares in his first week as PM (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

“We know a lot of the issues. People have been saying it for years and no one listened. Bills that land like a threat. A high street of shuttered units and rip-off prices.”

He added: "So here is what's coming. A third off bus fares. VAT off your electricity bill. Action next week on misleading discounts and pricing tricks. We're putting money back in people's pockets and giving communities the power they need to thrive. Good growth in every postcode. Hope in every heart.”

‌



As he returns from a short summer holiday this week, Mr Burnham is expected to renew his focus on the cost of living and travel around the nation before Parliament returns in early September. Insiders confirmed among the places the new Labour leader will visit will be Port Talbot, south Wales - an area reeling from over 2,000 job losses after the closure of a final blast furnace.

Reports have previously suggested Mr Burnham could head to parts of the country where his party has lost support in recent years including areas that voted Reform in 2024. No10 said he will sit down with families, shop owners and workers during the tour.

The visits will ultimately inform his work on a new 10-year plan for the country that Mr Burnham promised later this year in his first speech as Prime Minister. He said at the time it would lay out a “path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be” later in 2026.

‌



It follows a policy blitz in his first week in Downing with measures designed to give cash-strapped families breathing space on the cost of living. This included a promise to remove the VAT charged on electricity bills from October 1 - estimated to cost £850million - to knock £45 off the average bill.

There was also the decision to reintroduce the £2 bus fare cap to slash day-to-day travel costs for millions of passengers across England from January. The £2 cap was first introduced by the Tories in 2023, but funding was only put in place by Rishi Sunak ’s government until the end of 2024.

View 3 Images Andy Burnham at No10 North in Manchester during his first week as Prime Minister (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves hiked it to £3 as she battled to balance the books. The current cap, which applies to around 5,000 bus routes across England, was planned to last until March 2027.

In his second week as PM, Mr Burnham also began to grapple with some of the thorniest issues facing Britain including the broken social care sector, defence spending, and the staggering number of young people out of work, education and training. The PM has established No10 North in Manchester which Downing Street said was set up to get the government out of the Westminster bubble.

The summer tour - expected to begin this week - also comes amid evidence of a “Burnham bounce” in the national polls and closing the gap on Nigel Farage ’s Reform UK. Elections expert Professor Sir John Curtice told the BBC last week it was confirmed by Labour's comfortable victory in the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election, where Reform had been hoping for a major political upset in Labour's traditional heartland.

Article continues below

Sir John added: "Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down. But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence."

News.title: 'Coronation Street' rapist's cause of death behind bars confirmed
News.content:
'Coronation Street' rapist's cause of death behind bars confirmed

Andrew Davies, dubbed 'The Coronation Street rapist,' was handed 13 life sentences for raping 13 women and an additional 56 years for other offences after striking terror across the north

View 3 Images Andrew Davies, from Bolton, targeted lone women (Image: MEN)

The cause of death of a serial predator, who struck terror across the north of England, has been confirmed.

‌



Andrew Davies, from Bolton, targeted lone women after waiting for their husbands or fathers to leave the property in the morning.

‌



Davies, formerly known as Andrew Barlow and Andrew Longmire was given 13 life sentences for his vile crimes in 1988. He was released in 2023 after 34 years in prison, but was recalled to prison just six weeks later.

‌



The decision to release Davies, known as ‘the Coronation Street rapist,’ sparked public fury and the then Justice Secretary Dominic Raab intervened in a bid to prevent it. Just weeks after his release he was recalled to prison for breach of his licence conditions.

View 3 Images Davies, formerly known as Andrew Barlow and Andrew Longmire was given 13 life sentences for his crimes (Image: MEN)

News of Davies' death was reported in February this year but now a report by the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman has disclosed further details.

‌



Davies died from natural causes after contracting brain cancer, the Manchester Evening News reports. The report states: "In October 2017, Mr Andrew Davies was sentenced to life imprisonment for sexual offences. He died of brain cancer on 28 February 2026, at HMP Moorland. He was 69 years old. We offer our condolences to Mr Davies’ family and friends.

"The Ombudsman’s office wrote to Mr Davies’ next of kin to explain the investigation and to ask if they had any matters they wanted us to consider. They did not respond.

"One prisoner contacted us and raised concerns about the care Mr Davies received at Moorland. NHS England commissioned an independent clinical reviewer to review Mr Davies’ clinical care at Moorland.

‌



View 3 Images Andrew Davies, from Bolton, targeted lone women (Image: MEN)

"The clinical reviewer concluded that the clinical care Mr Davies received at Moorland was of a reasonable standard and was equivalent to that which he could have expected to receive in the community. She made four recommendations on issues unrelated to Mr Davies’ death which the Head of Healthcare will wish to address.

"The PPO investigator investigated the non-clinical issues relating to Mr Davies’ care. We did not find any non-clinical issues of concern. We make no recommendations. We shared our initial report with HMPPS and the prison’s healthcare provider, Practice Plus Group.

‌



"They found no factual inaccuracies. At the inquest, held on 8 April 2026, the Coroner concluded that Mr Davies died from natural causes."

Barlow was handed 11 life sentences in for raping 11 women and an additional 56 years for other offences at a 1988 trial. In 2010, and then again in 2017, he received two more life sentences after rapes he committed in 1981 and 1982 which were linked to him through advances in DNA technology.

As he had already surpassed his original 20-year tariff imposed in 1988 just another two years were added to his sentence in each case.

Article continues below

He was dubbed 'The Coronation Street rapist' as most of the victims were attacked in their own terraced homes in the north of England, the majority living in Greater Manchester. Two of the attacks took place in the street. He also struck in Cheshire, Staffordshire, Lancashire, and South Yorkshire in the early 1980s, and then again from August 1987 until January 1988 when he was arrested.

Barlow was sought by police in the 1980s over 11 of the rapes. During the hunt for him he evaded police at Leeds railway station and went on to shoot at two officers when he was finally arrested in Bebington, Merseyside. The officers were not injured and Longmire was later convicted of their attempted murder.

News.title: Search for Everest team to bring body known as 'Green Boots' home after 30 years frozen near summit
News.content:
Search for Everest team to bring body known as 'Green Boots' home after 30 years frozen near summit

WARNING: DISTRESSING CONTENT. Dorje Morup died on an expedition up Mount Everest over 30 years ago - his body is finally set to be returned to his family after his 'green boots' became a grim landmark

View 3 Images A man's body is set to be returned 30 years after he died on Mount Everest (file photo) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The frozen body of a man who perished on Mount Everest is set to be brought home after over 30 years.

‌



Dorje Morup died 27,890ft high up the mountain while on an expedition with the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) in May 1996. For 30 years h is body has remained in the same spot ever since, in full view of a main route, known to climbers as 'green boots'.

‌



He is one of around 200 people whose remains are left on the mountain in what is known as the "death zone", where temperatures can drop as low as -40C and oxygen levels are just a third of what they are at sea level. Their bodies act as macabre markers for climbers attempting to reach the summit.

‌



View 3 Images 'Green boots' has become a grim landmark for passing climbers (Image: WikiCommons)

Legendary mountaineer and ex-British soldier Nirmal Purja confirmed killed in Pakistan avalanche READ MORE :

The man was only identified as 48-year-old Dorje Morup, from Ladakh, India, earlier this year, with his body having previously assumed to be that of a different soldier who went missing on Everest. Now, his remains are set to be returned to his family after Indian authorities began a search for a specialist high-altitude recovery team.

The Indo-Tibetan Border Police said it hopes to bring the remains back to India by September, after which DNA testing would be carried out to firmly establish his identity. Nearly 350 people have died while climbing Mount Everest since it was first scaled by Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay in 1953

‌



Reacting to the news of the expedition to bring her husband's body, his wife Konchak Yangskit told the BBC: "On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there. When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

View 3 Images The body is now believed to be that of Dorje Morup (Image: Indo-Tibetan Border Police)

One barrier to the retrieval of the remains has come in its location on Everest’s Tibetan side, where access is controlled by Chinese authorities and climbing permits are rarely issued with most climbers choosing to ascend from the Nepalese side. China closed the mountain to foreign climbers during this year's spring climbing season, providing no explanation.

‌



Pemba Sherpa, founder of the Kathmandu-based Xtreme Climbers Treks and Expedition, said of the recovery mission last month: "It is not impossible to retrieve the body from Everest, but the first challenge is getting permission from the Chinese officials and then only can they proceed to bring the body down."

The Chinese side of the peak is also steeper and lacks the same level of support structures as the southern slope. Pemba Ongchu Sherpa explained: "It's really tough to get that body down even in [the] popular spring season, let alone the autumn [when weather is more unpredictable]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years. There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of m aking summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point."

Then there's the logistics of transporting a body down a mountainside. Green Boots would have to be physically carried down until climbers reached an altitude where the remains can be collected by helicopter or yaks and transported back to an airport. According to sherpas, bodies in iced covered climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are often frozen into awkward positions. There's also a risk the remains begin defrosting and decomposing as they descend.

‌



Dorje Morup's team was part of a 1996 expedition organized by the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), who aimed to become the first Indian crew to successfully reach the summit via the treacherous North Col route. The night before his historic expedition, Dorje promised his wife he would return a hero and make his country proud.

"He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak said. Despite Dorje's exerpeince with Himalayan trekking, his wife said she had a strange sense of foreboding that night, admitting: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again."

As they made their way to the peak, three of the six members of Dorje's expedition group turned back due to a snowstorm but he and two others, Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor kept going. But disaster struck as they descended as a blizzard hit, killing all three.

Article continues below

Only the body which became known as 'Green Boots' has ever been found. For years it was assumed that this was the body of Tsewang Paljor, but testimony from survivors of the 1996 expedition and the location of the climbers last radio contact has led authorities to believe the remains are Dorje's. An ITBP official, speaking anonymously, told BBC News Hindi that the clothes and climbing gesad had been key to identifying the body. They added: "We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time."

Today, all that remains of Dorje are his medals and trophies, along with a few old photos from his mountain adventures and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government stating that at 5.30pm on May 10, 1995, Dorje reached the summit of Everest. To go alongside this, the family plan to keep a symbol of Dorje's legacy at their home when he is returned, his eldest son Punchok Dorjai explained: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots."

News.title: Man accused of Brit's suitcase murder in Greece 'turned back on faith' before her death
News.content:
Man accused of Brit's suitcase murder in Greece 'turned back on faith' before her death

The body of Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was discovered in a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens on July 18, and Afghan refugee and Christian convert Sharif Ahmadzai has been charged with her murder

View 4 Images Sharif Ahmadzai, who is suspected of killing Elisabeth-Jane Ross, and his wife Alaina Hall (Image: FACEBOOK)

The man accused of killing British woman Elisabeth-Jane Ross, who was found dead inside a suitcase in Greece, reportedly “turned his back on his Christian faith” before her death.

‌



Afghan boxer Sharif Ahmadzai has been charged with homicide with intent over the death of 38-year-old Elisabeth-Jane, known as Lisa, whose body was discovered inside a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens on July 18.

‌



The claims about Ahmadzai's faith and behaviour before Lisa's death have been reported by the Daily Mail, which spoke to two evangelical Christians who said his wife Alaina Hall had confided in them about concerns she had regarding her husband's changing behaviour.

‌



According to the newspaper, Alaina told the pair that Ahmadzai had become more distant from his Christian faith and was spending more time boxing and with friends. The sources also claimed she had become concerned about him spending time in bars in Athens.

View 4 Images Elisabeth Jane Ross, also known as Lisa, was found by a homeless man on July 18 (Image: Facebook)

Ahmadzai fled Afghanistan in 2016 and is understood to have converted to Christianity after meeting Alaina through charity work in Greece. The couple run a charity called Love Every Nation, which supports homeless people and refugees in Athens.

‌



Lisa had also been carrying out charity work in Greece as a Christian aid worker and had met Alaina through volunteering and church meetings. Alaina told investigators she and Lisa had become friends after meeting in February.

She reportedly told police she last saw Lisa on July 12. When she later asked her husband when he had seen Lisa, he allegedly said they had last spoken on July 15, when Lisa had asked him to accompany her while delivering a Bible.

Alaina also reportedly told investigators that she woke shortly after midnight on July 15 and found Ahmadzai was not at home. She said she checked his location on her mobile phone.

‌



Ahmadzai was initially arrested on weapons offences before prosecutors charged him with homicide with intent. He also faces allegations of stealing more than €10,000 (around £8,500) from Lisa's bank accounts using her bank cards.

View 4 Images Sharif Ahmadzai was a keen boxer (Image: INSTAGRAM)

Greek authorities say Ahmadzai has admitted moving Lisa's body but denies killing her.

‌



His lawyer, Christos Erdos, confirmed his client did not answer questions during Thursday's hearing.

Following the hearing, a judge ordered Ahmadzai to remain in pre-trial detention while prosecutors continue gathering evidence ahead of future court proceedings. The allegations against Ahmadzai have not been proven in court.

He was later escorted from court by masked police officers and driven away.

‌



Investigators previously said Ahmadzai became a suspect after officers examined CCTV footage recorded close to where Lisa's body was discovered.

View 4 Images Elisabeth Jane Ross was reportedly known to Sharif Ahmadzai through his wife Alaina Hall (Image: Facebook)

Police believe she died several days before she was found, during a period when temperatures in Athens reached 36C. She was formally identified using fingerprint evidence.

Article continues below

Lisa travelled to Greece on June 26 and had initially been staying with friends in the port district of Piraeus.

The Foreign and Commonwealth Office said earlier: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”

A Police Scotland spokesperson previously said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece. Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”

News.title: Mums and babies risk lives on mega-dinghies in desperate bid to get to UK
News.content:
This is the human face of the Channel boats crisis, desperate people on the final leg of a journey that could kill them.

Our exclusive images show young children, including some in pushchairs, being bussed to board mega-dinghies to get to Britain. Our investigators tracked a group of around 50 migrants, including small children and women earlier this week as they travelled around 40 miles south-west from France’s largest migrant camp at Loon-Plage, near Dunkirk, to Ecault Forest, close to Boulogne.

The group had paid around £1,200 each to make the final leg of their journey to the UK. They also paid extra for lifejackets, sold at stalls in the Loon-Plage camp for up to €50 (£42) – almost double the price in nearby shops.

View 8 Images Katie Sweetingham, head of operations at Care4Calais (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Express)

‌



English Channel horror as 157 migrants capsize on flaming boat with France and UK launching rescue mission READ MORE :

Three migrants die crossing the Channel after busiest day this year READ MORE :

Katie Sweetingham, Head of Operations at charity Care4Calais, says she has seen increasing numbers of women and children, including babies, at the camp since the UK government indefinitely paused family reunion applications in September last year. She said: “Lots of women and children would use that scheme to be reunited with their loved ones in the UK and now that option is not available. So they have to get into a boat and make that dangerous crossing.”

The journey we saw the migrants make on Thursday seemed complicated. After being taken from the camp to a bus stop in Loon-Plage, the group boarded a bus to Gravelines. Following a lengthy wait, they then took a second bus from Gravelines to Calais, before boarding a train to Boulogne, where they got on another bus to the edge of the forest.

View 8 Images Migrants in Boulogne where they were preparing to take their third bus journey of the day (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Express)

On getting off the final bus, they made their way along hiking paths to a makeshift dwelling inside the protected natural site, which includes various camping spots for caravans. They appeared to be being guided by a tall man, believed to be Kurdish, who had a distinctive tattoo on his right hand.

‌



French police, including armed gendarmes, followed the migrants throughout the four-hour journey, including walking with them into the forest. But they made no attempt to stop them.

Good weather has led to perfect sailing conditions so far this summer, causing a spike in crossing attempts by gangs. Four migrants, including three women, have died in separate boat tragedies in the Channel in recent days. And with the favourable conditions now expected to continue until at least September, there are fears of more tragedies. Investigators say traffickers are increasingly exploiting the Opal Coast, south of Boulogne, to launch dangerously overloaded rubber boats following a crackdown further north in Calais and Dunkirk.

View 8 Images Stalls, linked to the smuggling gangs, at Loon-Plage migrant camp are selling life jackets for 50 Euros (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Mirror)

They use new mega-dinghies bought from manufacturers in China. Despite being completely unfit for open seas, the boats are being used to transport more than 150 migrants at a time, netting the gangs up to £200,000 for a single trip. Ordering a mega-dinghy previously took months and involved a 5,500-mile journey by road, via countries including Kazakhstan and Turkey, costing traffickers at least £10,000.

‌



However, we can reveal at least one factory is now offering direct delivery by plane to France, in packages measuring just 2m x 1m x 1m. The vessels are advertised online as Huge Large Super Inflatable Pontoon Rescue Boats, and cost just £1,200. But they are billed as being designed for 40 people, not 150. The maximum delivery time is just two weeks.

View 8 Images Police patrol the beach at Équihen Plage on the lookout for migrants trying to board mega dinghies (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

Katie said: “We’ve heard about the bigger dinghies from the people we support. It’s a recent change. It just goes to show that all of the border security measures, largely funded by the UK, don’t do their stated aim of stopping the crossings. All they do is make people that are organising the crossings change their business model, which is now the larger boats, making it much more dangerous for the people that are attempting crossings.”

Katie says she and her team regularly meet children as young as 13 trying to cross to Britain without adult supervision. She said: “It’s usually going to be those younger people that are targeted for driving the boat and then on entry to the UK they’re much more likely to be criminalised and not believed for their age.”

‌



View 8 Images A group of Iraqi Kurdish migrants walk down the main road into Equihen Plage, a popular migrant beach for onward small boat transport to Britain (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

A week last Thursday, a boat overturned in the water near Ecault Forest, causing the death of a man and leading to the near-drowning of a baby. The same day, three women in their 20s, 30s and 40s, drowned after an inflatable dinghy with more than 100 people on board capsized near Loon-Plage.

Katie said: “More people are dying trying to make the journey. A lot of them speak to us and say they’ve been on a boat and they’ve seen their friends die in front of them, but then they will say ‘what else can I do?’ There’s no other way for that person to be able to reach safety in the UK to be able to gain asylum other than to repeat that journey again and try again.”

8 View 8 Images Migrants walking down the main road into Equihen Plage on Saturday (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com) 8 View 8 Images Migrants were also seen wandering the many trails inside Écault Forest while waiting for an opportunity to board boats to Britain (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

‌



Figures have just revealed the average number of migrants crammed per boat has more than doubled over five years. Analysis found 66 migrants on average have been packed on to each of the 219 vessels to cross the Channel successfully this year. They carried 14,561 passengers in total. An average of 27 per boat was recorded for the whole of 2021, when 1,064 vessels carrying 28,526 migrants made it to the Kent coast.

A source said: “These so-called mega-dinghies are hugely profitable and the smugglers are getting hold of them very easily. Their emergence means a huge number of people can be moved at one time, but always in extremely and increasingly dangerous circumstances. Frankly, it is a nightmare development for the authorities.”

An Egyptian man yesterday began a one-year prison sentence in France after being convicted of trying to smuggle a record 173 migrants into Britain on a 40ft mega-dinghy that burst into flames in the Channel. An Iraqi-born people-smuggler, named by police as Rasoul Halo, was on Tuesday also imprisoned for a year, for smuggling an inflatable boat on to a beach. Halo, who was found with three passports including a British one, claimed he was just helping a friend with a delivery.

News.title: Andy Burnham to embark on cost of living tour through the UK
News.content:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales â with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living â although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles â like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off â must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme â including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

The Conservatives said the government's "tax hikes and red tape are hammering our high streets".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said: "This is breathtaking hypocrisy from Burnhamâ¦ they are forcing businesses to close, destroying jobs and driving up prices for the public.

"Meanwhile, Labour are plotting to release dangerous criminals onto our streets, leaving people feeling unsafe in their communities."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper said struggling high street businesses "need more than a new PM embarking on a vanity tour this summer".

She said the PM should adopt the Lib Dem plan for high streets: "That means reversing the damaging jobs tax, delivering an emergency VAT cut for hospitality, replacing broken business rates and cracking down on the ghost landlords leaving our shop fronts vacant."

Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "If Andy Burnham wants to help people with the cost of living, he should scrap the green levies and taxes on energy bills and rule out tax rises at the Budget."

News.title: Fifa criticises campaign to oust president Infantino
News.content:
Fifa has strongly criticised what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and its president Gianni Infantino.

The statement follows a Daily Telegraph report, external which claimed Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment by Uefa after he had an affair while he was its general secretary.

A Fifa spokesperson told the Telegraph Infantino "strongly denies" the allegations and that they are "categorically untrue".

Fifa has now itself hit out at "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims", adding that "speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure from Uefa and European football associations over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

Uefa has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness on Friday called on the Swiss-Italian to resign.

European football's governing body says its threat to boycott Fifa events remains on the table, adding that assurances the FFE plan could not be revived have not been received.

"The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa's Member Associations and continues to serve with their mandate," Fifa said in its statement on Saturday.

"It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president.

"Those who do not have the support of Fifa's member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa's established democratic processes."

Opposition to Infantino is largely from within Europe.

The Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa member countries.

Infantino is also unanimously backed by the 54 nations of the Confederation of African Football (Caf).

News.title: Killed a month after his wedding - why PC Andrew Harper's death touched so many
News.content:
On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.

Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty.

"Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.

They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.

In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.

They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".

They had been about to go on their honeymoon.

But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.

The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers â Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole â will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.

As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more â at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.

PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.

Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.

PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.

He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.

During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.

His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.

PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.

The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.

It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.

But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.

News.title: Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites
News.content:
Up in the hills above the Roman columns of the ancient site of Sebastia, in the occupied West Bank, are olive fields that have been cultivated for generations by Palestinian families.

One of the landowners, Abu Mudif, says he has received notification that his land is part of a tranche of about 450 acres that the Israeli authorities are taking possession of in order, they say, to protect and develop the site for a major new national park.

Typically, Palestinian landowners receive little or no payment for such land expropriation. And even when it is offered, most refuse it as they see accepting it as giving recognition and legitimacy to the loss of what they see as their patrimony.

It's a vital income for Abu Mudif to lose of course, but it goes deeper than that for him.

News.title: Sturgeon hasn't spoken to Murrell since he was jailed for embezzling SNP funds
News.content:
Sturgeon also told Dale that she only discovered Murrell was due to plead guilty a week before his first public court appearance.

It later emerged he had been negotiating his plea for months, a fact which she said "hit me like a tonne of bricks".

Sturgeon said: "He was still lying to me right up until the day he pled guilty."

The former first minister added: "He was very isolated over that period, he very rarely left the house, he wasn't communicative, I was a bit worried about his well-being and his mental health.

"And then, now I think: 'What a mug, why were you worried about him?' He didn't worry about me. He didn't worry at all about what he was doing.

"What he has subjected me to is beyond anything I could ever have comprehended.

"I don't understand why he did it, he had no need to do it, I don't think I will ever understand his motivations.

"But whatever that motivation was, he could not have stopped and ever thought about me.

"But I was, until recently, still worrying about him."

Sturgeon - who had stepped down as first minister in March 2023 - was arrested In June 2023 but was later told that she was no longer under investigation.

The former first minister announced her separation from Murrell last year.

News.title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
News.content:
There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.

The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.

Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina.

He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.

A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.

People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.

Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.

NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.

Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.

Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.

This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more.

"I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.

For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.

But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.

Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."

When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says.

"My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.

There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.

But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.

For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.

When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.

Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.

News.title: Your university clearing survival guide ahead of results day
News.content:
At first, he wanted to take a gap year after his A-levels so did not apply for university, but was persuaded to go by family and friends after achieving "great grades".

On the day, with the help of his A-level teachers, he filled in a Ucas form, applied to six universities via clearing and picked the University of Manchester to study politics and modern history.

"The good thing about clearing is that you can apply to as many universities as you want, unlike with Ucas, where you are limited to five," he says.

"That was definitely stress-relieving," he says.

For those on the fence about university, Nasir recommends people put in a Ucas application "just in case" to avoid the stress of results day.

That's a piece of advice that is echoed by Wade.

"You will need a referee, which is why I'd suggest doing it now," she says.

"Let's say [you've] got to email the teacher, the teacher's got to add a reference, then Ucas only gets sent once all of those parts are sent together."

Nasir says he wished he was more prepared for clearing, and advises students to write down some notes on location, accommodation and cost for each university you contact.

"Make sure you know whether you qualify before calling," he says.

"With my university I was required to have a specific A-level, so make sure you meet the requirements."

News.title: Raw images, no filters: Why MySpace fans want it back as relaunch hinted
News.content:
MySpace launched in 2003 and quickly became a cultural hub, helping artists like Arctic Monkeys, Adele, and Nicki Minaj find early audiences.

But its highly customised pages, auto-playing music, and busy layouts eventually became a liability.

Facebook's cleaner, simpler design pulled users away, and MySpace struggled through redesigns and ownership changes before fading from mainstream use.

Marketing experts say any comeback will depend on learning from that history.

Dr Alexa Fox, a marketing professor at the University of Akron, says the platform was a "first mover" in social media, but one that became too complex for many users.

She believes MySpace's original strengths â music, creativity, and personal expression â could still resonate, but only with more accessible design.

"It could be more user-friendly, with less coding involved," she says.

Alex Mills, a social media strategist who has led campaigns for Spotify and Adobe, says the very thing people are nostalgic for, a feed without algorithms, was also "the thing that killed it."

"People still want a feed," Mills says. "They just want a better one than the ones optimising for rage bait."

Kevin McClary, head of performance marketing at Gorilla 76, believes MySpace should not try to compete directly with Meta, TikTok, or X.

"They can be successful and sustainable even as a niche platform," he says, arguing it should be rooted in 2000s culture.

McClary says leaning into MySpace's music identity could be a smart move, from profile songs to 2000s-themed festivals and merchandise.

He believes the audience could be broader than former users, with younger generations embracing the early-2000s aesthetics they never experienced firsthand.

"You see younger generations now buying old point-and-shoot digital cameras, MP3 players, even film cameras," McClary says. "They clearly have an interest in the past."

MySpace could meet users where that trend is growing by becoming a place rooted in a "specific time," he says. He noted that creators making 2000s-style content on other platforms are often at the "mercy" of algorithms.

Fox agrees that differentiation is essential.

"MySpace shouldn't hang their hat on features other platforms already dominate," Fox says, pointing to Reels and short-form videos.

Popular formats can be added, she says, but they should not define the platform.

She also sees an opportunity to offer a calmer experience. Today's feeds, she notes, are "algorithmic-driven AI, constantly in your face."

A platform where users have more control, or simply feel less overwhelmed, could stand out in a crowded market.

For fans like Hawkins and Kristin, the appeal is emotional as much as practical. Both say they would return if MySpace kept its original spirit.

For now, its comeback exists mostly as a promise â a reminder of a time when social media felt a little less polished and a lot more personal.

"Are you still gonna have that same feeling?" Hawkins says. "Are you still gonna feel like, 'oh my god, somebody loves me?'"

News.title: Simon Levy victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures'
News.content:
Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.

Andrea Simon called for a review on the "failure to monitor him appropriately" when the 40-year-old was known to police as a sexual predator.

British Transport Police said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.

Meanwhile, the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant is facing a misconduct investigation.

On Friday, Levy was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London while he was being monitored by the Met Police for being a convicted sex offender. He had previously committed a string of sex attacks.

The BBC reported how a series of grave failings by police, prosecutors and the courts left Levy free to murder, rape and sexually assault women.

Levy is due to be sentenced on Wednesday.

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."

Stephenson said a lovely evening with friends had turned into a horrible morning.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites," she said.

"It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realised what had happened."

News.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
News.content:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple in a statement said they were "taking some time apart as we work through very difficult personal challenges".

"This has been an incredibly painful and emotional journey for us both and it certainly wasn't an easy decision," they said in a joint post shared on their Instagram accounts.

The couple said James had moved out the family home some time ago and they "don't know exactly what the future holds".

"Right now, more than anything we ask for kindness, empathy and a little privacy as we work through this as a family."

The couple's manager Vickie White had prevously said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.

News.title: Charity watchdog investigates aid charity over alleged Hamas links
News.content:
A UK-based aid charity is being investigated by counter-terror police and the charity watchdog over alleged links to Hamas.

The Charity Commission launched an inquiry into Muslim faith-based charity Al-Khair Foundation on Friday.

Counter Terror Policing London (CTP) also confirmed investigations into the charity, with two search warrants on addresses in Croydon, South London.

The foundation said it is "co-operating fully" with the inquiry and had filed a serious incident report with the watchdog before it was launched.

A spokesperson for the foundation said: "Everywhere we work we are firmly committed to ensuring that the funds entrusted to us by our generous donors are used for their intended purpose: meeting the humanitarian needs of poor and marginalised people in the communities we serve.

"Al-Khair Foundation is deeply committed to supporting those in need in Gaza. Our significant support over many years has included providing food parcels, hot meals, clean water, medical aid, shelter materials, winter assistance and orphan and family support."

The Al-Khair Foundation provides emergency relief and developmental support in "some of the world's most impoverished areas", according to its website.

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organisation by the UK and US governments.

It comes after last week Mohammad Yousef Hasna, 45, from Istanbul, Turkey, was arrested in the UK over US accusations of conspiring to funnel money and supplies to Hamas through a "sham charity".

The US Department of Justice did not name the "sham charity" in their press release.

The Al-Khair foundation maintains that Hasna is not an employee but works with one of its global partners to enable the delivery of aid around the world.

Hasna is being held following his arrest by the UK's National Crime Agency (NCA) and pending extradition proceedings before he can be taken to New York to face the US charges.

The US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York alleged Hasna used his senior role at a "purported global humanitarian organisation to coordinate directly with Hamas's senior leadership regarding the delivery of funds and supplies to Gaza, and the distribution of those funds and supplies at Hamas leadership's instructions".

Hasna is charged with conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to finance terrorism and financing terrorism.

Each charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, the US Department of Justice said.

US Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said: "The money that flows from sham charities like the one described in the complaint fuels Hamas's terrorist activities, including the atrocities the group committed on October 7".

The Charity Commission said the Al-Khair Foundation recorded an income of more than Â£74m in the financial year ending 31 July 2025. The commission added it was made aware of the allegations against Hasna and "immediately started examining the serious concerns raised".

"The commission has now escalated its engagement to a statutory inquiry," the commission added.

Al-Khair is also subject to a legal order restricting some financial transactions being made without the consent of the Charity Commission.

News.title: Hundreds flying out of Birmingham Airport left without luggage
News.content:
She described seeing a "build up" of luggage at the airport, after problems with the luggage belt, but had been assured by staff that it would be loaded on to the plane.

But on arrival at Dalaman they were told by the pilot that no bags had been loaded.

"We have heard nothing about compensation, no communication when our luggage is expected, we've heard nothing about who is liable for it. Is it the airport? Is it TUI? Is it our travel insurance? Who are we meant to go to? We've had nothing from anybody", Chapman said.

"It's just radio silence from the airport, apart from literally telling people 'we've got an issue'".

The first day of their holiday was spent travelling to a shopping centre to buy essentials for "for the next few days" but she added "we have no idea how long this is going to last".

"There are families all over the world at the moment with nothing and no idea of what's going on," she said.

"It's really important that Birmingham Airport are held accountable, and sort this out."

News.title: Man guilty of fatal shooting of teen outside club
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of fatally shooting an 18-year-old outside a Wembley nightclub.

Tyrece Balcha was found with gunshot wounds outside the Crystal Club in Atlantic Crescent at about 05:30 GMT on 21 September 2025. He was taken to hospital, where he died four days later.

A jury at the Old Bailey found Ashley Wallace, 40, of Shenley Road, Southwark, guilty of murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

At the same trial, two men were found not guilty of murder. A woman was cleared of possession of a firearm, possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, and perverting the course of justice. The jury did not reach a verdict on a fourth man.

CCTV footage showed that Balcha had been involved in an altercation inside the club before being followed outside and shot.

Wallace fled the scene in a vehicle and was arrested on 25 September after police traced the car to south-east London.

A revolver carrying Wallace's DNA was found inside the vehicle, and investigators established that the bullet recovered from the murder scene had been fired from the gun.

News.title: Siân Phillips to step back from acting aged 93 after memory issues
News.content:
One of Wales' most celebrated actresses, Dame SiÃ¢n Phillips, is stepping back from full-scale stage acting after experiencing memory issues during rehearsals.

The 93-year-old made the decision after struggling to remember her lines while preparing for a recent production, according to The Times.

However, Phillips said she would continue performing in smaller projects, including a production with Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Her career has spanned more than 80 years across stage, television and film.

Phillips told The Times she decided to stop taking on major stage productions after struggling to remember her lines during rehearsals for Atonement at Chichester Festival Theatre earlier this year.

According to the newspaper, she said she would continue performing in her show It's All Greek and is also due to appear in Samuel Beckett's Rockaby for Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Born in Betws, near Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, in 1933, Phillips grew up speaking Welsh before learning English by listening to the radio.

She began performing as a child, appearing on Welsh-language radio from the age of 11, before studying at the University of Wales and later winning a scholarship to the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.

She performed in radio productions such as The Archers and an adaptation of John le Carre's Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy, opposite Sir Alec Guinness.

Before her acting career took off, she worked for BBC Wales as a bilingual announcer and newsreader.

Phillips went on to become one of Britain's most acclaimed actresses, appearing in productions including Doctor Who, Calendar Girls, Dune, and I, Claudius.

She won a Bafta for her portrayal of Livia in the BBC's I, Claudius and received a Tony Award nomination for playing the title role in Marlene.

She was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 2000 for services to drama, and then a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in 2016.

News.title: Todd Blanche as Trump’s new attorney general is a ‘red alert’ for abortion rights, groups warn
News.content:

Reproductive health advocates fear newly confirmed Attorney General Todd Blanche will usher in a new wave of restrictions on abortion — even in states where it is legal.

Blanche’s confirmation “is a red alert for reproductive rights,” according to Nancy Northup, president and CEO of the Center for Reproductive Rights. “The Attorney General’s job is to fairly and faithfully enforce the law, but Blanche appears willing to contort it to score wins for political allies,” she said Saturday.

Blanche has “openly vowed to use that power to ban abortion,” Gowri Buddiga, interim managing director for the group Free & Just, said in a statement shared with The Independent Saturday.

“From promising to restrict access to medication abortion through the mail, to gutting protections for patients and providers, Blanche will roll back access to care everywhere even in states where abortion is currently protected,” Buddiga said.

Blanche, who was confirmed in the early morning hours on Saturday by a narrow 50-49 vote, alarmed abortion advocates after leaked audio captured Trump’s former criminal defense attorney vowing to make the 2022 Supreme Court decision overturning the right to an abortion “permanent in every single state.”

open image in gallery Abortion rights groups fear newly confirmed Attorney General Todd Blanche will restrict access to the procedure nationwide, after leaked audio caught Blanche telling faith leaders he was gearing up for a ‘permanent’ victory on abortion ( Reuters )

“We don’t have complete victory yet, but we will have victory, and victory will be soon, and it will be permanent,” Blanche said, according to Politico, which obtained the now-deleted clip.

“If states have said, ‘We are going to protect the unborn and we’re going to protect every life from the moment of conception,’ we’re putting practices and policies in place so that other states and other organizations can’t attack that,” he reportedly added. “They can’t do things like they’re doing with mailing in mail-order drugs.”

The Independent has contacted the Department of Justice for comment.

The Justice Department previously told The Independent that the comments “need to be understood in their full context, which was with respect to mail order abortion drugs, not a broader expansion of federal control over states.”

Much to the chagrin of anti-abortion campaigners, abortions have actually increased since the constitutional right to abortion care was struck down at the Supreme Court, thanks to a mix of expanded telehealth access, Biden-era policies and blue state “shield laws” protecting physicians who provide abortion care.

While much of the attention in Blanche’s confirmation was directed at a now-abandoned $1.8 billion“slush fund” for the president’s political allies and a provision that shields the president from IRS investigations, Blanche’s appointment battle suggests the Trump administration could pursue more restrictions on abortion access.

open image in gallery Republicans are pushing the DOJ to settle cases challenging access to mifepristone, a commonly used abortion pill ( AFP/Getty )

Under questioning, he committed to reviewing the the Justice Department’s interpretation of the 1873 Comstock Act, which makes it illegal to send a variety of objects including “abortion-causing articles” via mail.

A 2022 Justice Department opinion held that the law doesn’t inherently bar sending abortion medication, given that “there are manifold ways in which recipients in every state may lawfully use such drugs, including to produce an abortion.”

On the campaign trail, Donald Trump described regulation around mail-order abortion drugs as a state issue, rather than a federal one, adding that he wouldn’t use the 19th century law to crack down on abortion access.

“The federal government should have nothing to do with this issue,” he said in 2024.

Republicans in the Senate have also pushed the federal government to settle lawsuits around mifepristone, a widely used abortion drug.

During his confirmation hearing, Blanche pointed to the FDA’s ongoing review of mifepristone. In 2023, the Biden administration ended in-person dispensing requirements around the drug, prompting challenges in Republican states.

“We have to have studies that we can defend in court,” he told senators in July.

In May, the Supreme Court continued to block nationwide restrictions on mifepristone after a conservative appeals court cut off mail-order and telehealth access the drug, threatening access to millions of patients.

The president has vowed to be “the most pro-life and pro-family president in American history.”

In 2022, the Supreme Court, thanks to the conservative supermajority Trump helped appoint, overturned the landmark 1973 decision in Roe v Wade, which had established a constitutional right to an abortion.

News.title: Extremist 764 group allegedly linked to Southern California hospital bomb threat
News.content:

Federal authorities were investigating a bomb threat at Huntington Hospital in Pasadena on Saturday after an evacuation was prompted by a caller who allegedly identified himself as a member of the extremist online group 764.

The call was received at around 5:50 a.m. Friday, according to Pasadena spokeswoman Lisa Derderian.

The Pasadena Police Department said the caller claimed multiple explosive devices had been placed throughout the hospital and alleged that two additional suspects were heading to the facility in a stolen vehicle. The caller also claimed the suspects intended to shoot people with automatic rifles.

Officers responded to the hospital and worked with security to secure all entrances while establishing a strong law enforcement presence around the facility.

Police set up a command post in the parking lot of a nearby business and called in multiple K9 units. The Pasadena Fire Department also responded and remained on standby to assist if needed.

The caller also claimed the suspects intended to shoot people with automatic rifles ( Andrew Leyden/Getty Images )

Pasadena and Glendale police K9 units searched and cleared all publicly accessible areas of the hospital but found no explosive devices, police said.

As a precaution, incoming emergency traffic was diverted to nearby hospitals after the bomb threat was reported. Once the hospital was deemed safe, normal operations resumed.

The hospital was declared safe shortly after 9 a.m. Friday.

Although no one was injured in Friday’s threat, Derderian said such incidents are “very disruptive” and divert valuable resources from law enforcement and fire response teams.

The FBI has described 764 as "a violent online group made-up of individuals who seek to coerce and manipulate children into engaging in unspeakable acts against themselves, animals, and other children, even suicide."

Members of the group exist throughout the United States and around the world and operate on social media, gaming apps and online platforms, authorities said. Officials added that the group is also known to engage in "swatting" -- placing false emergency calls to trigger armed police raids.

Southern California has previously been targeted by swatting calls involving hospitals. In April, a bomb threat at Southern California Hospital in the Culver City area prompted a response from explosives-detection K-9 units and was ultimately determined to be a swatting incident. No explosive device was found.
