World.title: Historic farm's sale to carbon credit company raises community ire
World.content:
The sale of a historic Victorian high country cattle station to a carbon fund manager has raised concerns among residents and a federal MP about the property's future.

Cobungra Station, which has been farming cattle for more than 170 years near Omeo, has been sold to specialist carbon fund and asset manager Silva Capital.

Silva Capital creates and manages Australian Carbon Credit Units projects as part of the federal government's Carbon Credit Scheme.

Credits are generated through land reforestation and other agricultural projects that support the transition to net zero.

Carbon farming projects have become common in Australia, as companies look for quality carbon capture projects. (ABC News: Melanie Arnost, file photo)

The fund has confirmed plans to transform the station, running a carbon project alongside cattle farming.

"It's been done in several locations across Victoria and throughout Australia," Silva Capital co-managing director Raphael Wood said.

"What we've aimed to prove here is that food and fibre and carbon sequestration biodiversity can go hand in hand and create a more sustainable agricultural system," he said.

The transformation will see more native vegetation planted on the farm.

Raphael Wood says the fund will work with the local community to ensure all concerns around the Cobungra sale are addressed. (Supplied: Stephen Blake)

"We work with local experts, local community, the people who've worked that station before, to learn from them how to maximise the productivity and bring in new science and new techniques, for open woodland integrated with pasture to improve hopefully the productivity on site," Mr Wood said.

What's lost?

The deal has been approved by the Foreign Investment Review Board, and the sale of the farm is imminent.

However, some community members fear the project will result in a shift in Cobungra's identity.

Dianne Carroll is a local historian from nearby Omeo.

She said Cobungra had special significance for the local area.

"Slowly we are seeing the demise of many farms and that history is an important part of our culture, and it should be retained," Ms Carroll said.

"I'm not arguing against the conservation or protection of our environment, but I'm questioning whether productive, historical, significant country is the appropriate place to permanently convert land for the generation of carbon credits," she said.

The Coalition has called on the government to reject the proposal.

Cobungra lies in the electorate of the federal opposition agriculture spokesperson Darren Chester.

He said the decision to allow the proposal distorted the market for anyone who wished to buy land for traditional agricultural purposes.

"The individual or the farming organisation who might want to come along and continue to use the property for just mainstream agricultural production will be outbid by an organisation relying on government subsidies and schemes to fund their purchases," Mr Chester said.

Darren Chester says selling farms for carbon projects sets a worrying precedent. (Supplied: Darren Chester)

Mr Chester drew on the recent example of the sale of Tasmania's biggest farm, Rushy Lagoon, to a British investor, which was partially funded through the federal government's Clean Energy Finance Corporation.

He said the cumulative impact of large farms being acquired under the government's model deserved closer consideration.

"What is the long-term ambition for these carbon credit type sales? How many millions of hectares of productive agricultural land will we lose before it's in the national interest?" he said.

Mr Wood said the fund was looking forward to engaging with the local community about any concerns they had over the process.

"We intend to reach out to the community and start engaging and learning from the community about how we can maintain the agricultural productivity of Cobungra, and introduce them to what we are trying to achieve with Silva and Cobungra," he said.

A chance to diversify

Not all agree that carbon farming and traditional agriculture are at odds.

Farmers for Climate Action chief executive Verity Morgan-Schmidt said carbon farming could coexist with traditional farming, and helped diversify farmers' income.

Verity Morgan-Schmidt says carbon farming and more traditional farming can co-exist. (Supplied: Farmers for Climate Action)

"To me, that represents the opportunity that is actually increasingly coming down the pipeline for Australian producers to be able to diversify their income streams and actually, over the longer term, look to strengthen the resilience of their properties and regions as well," she said.

"It's really about a revenue diversification opportunity for farmers, provided we get their methodologies right and make sure that farmers are able to manage the access into that market as well."

The Clean Energy Finance Corporation has confirmed it is not involved in the purchase of Cobungra.

The Federal Government has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Trams are running but the Gold Coast's light rail fight is not over
World.content:
After $1.55 billion and four years of disruptive construction, the Gold Coast's latest mass transit system has finally begun taking passengers.

Light rail stage 3 has connected the bustling shopping precinct of Broadbeach to the stunning beaches of Burleigh Heads.

The state government estimates two million passengers will use the network every month but the light rail has become a symbol of the city's struggle to manage population growth.

Locals know the trams carry big change.

Decades in the making

Urban planning consultant Ned Wales worked at Gold Coast City Council in the mid-2000s, as detailed planning for light rail began.

"Light rail has a dedicated right of way; you get the reliability in terms of timing and scheduling," he said.

"[It's] not cheap but it's certainly been well worth it."

Associate Professor Ned Wales from Bond University. (ABC: Glenn Mullane)

The first stage — a 13-kilometre line from Gold Coast University Hospital to Broadbeach — took three years to build and cost $1.61 billion in today's dollars.

The former Labor state government initially estimated the 6.7km stage 3 would cost $709 million.

That has since blown-out to $1.55 billion.

Mr Wales, now an Assistant Professor of Sustainable Development at Bond University, said light rail required costly upgrades to underground sewer and water infrastructure — with "many, many moving parts" involved.

An aerial shot of the Stage 3 light rail construction, looking north from Miami to Mermaid Beach. (Supplied: GoldLinQ)

In September 2025, light rail operator GoldLinQ said 48km of utilities had been relocated or upgraded and 137 power poles installed to build 60 per cent of stage 3.

GoldLinQ chair John Witheriff said crews were uncovering decades-old infrastructure, including broken asbestos-cement water pipes, adding unexpected delays.

"We've got no idea what's underground in our city and we've got no idea how long the stuff's been in there and when it's all going to break up," he said at the time.

Disruption and reflection

Those disruptions came at a cost for many businesses along the route.

Jess Firkin relocated his vintage clothing shop from the light rail route in Mermaid Beach south to Miami last year.

"When something happens to you, you're very quick to make judgement and point figures," he said.

"But that doesn't get the bills paid."

Jess Firkin at his old shopfront at Mermaid Beach last year, prior to moving. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Now about 100 metres off the new light rail route, Mr Firkin said his trade had increased by 70 per cent.

"As much as it does suck for things to happen outside of your control, there are always actions you can take to help rectify those situations," he said.

"I would really like it to end on a positive note and really emphasise that business owners need to take accountability and that's my biggest lesson."

Construction of light rail at Mermaid Beach, in April 2025. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

Locals Raeleigh and Russell Olive said the construction process has been "a real mess".

"The restrictions on getting in and out of Burleigh [are] … gone and it looks good again," Ms Olive said.

"It's one of our favourite places to come, so it's nice to know that other people will be enjoying it as well."

But Mr Olive said "it would have been a great idea" to extend the line further south to the airport.

Opposition builds, plans get scrapped

Light rail was not meant to end with stage 3.

Stage 4 would have connected Burleigh Heads to the airport, described as a critical part of the entire network by urban planners.

But the cancellation of stage 4 came about after once-sleepy coastal villages along the proposed route became the focus of intense high-rise development.

The light rail ends at Burleigh Heads, instead of extending further south to the airport, as planned. (Graphic: ABC News)

Opposition grew in suburbs such as Palm Beach, where "Trams Outta Palmy" signs appeared outside homes and shops.

Even surfing great Mick Fanning voiced his disapproval online.

While he supported stage 4, Mr Wales said "the downside is gentrification".

"Real estate values increase particularly around tram stations," he said. "That may lead to some displacement of those on lower socio-economic incomes."

Opposition to light rail on the southern Gold Coast has been vocal, with protests seen here in 2021. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale)

The LNP government cancelled stage 4 last year, citing local opposition and an estimated cost of $5.7 billion to $9.8 billion.

But on Friday, Queensland Labor senator Murray Watt said the state had not given the Commonwealth a firm stage 4 business case, making it "impossible to say exactly what that cost would be".

The state has preserved the light rail corridor along the southern Gold Coast, leaving the door open for a future government to revive the project.

What's next?

A network of larger buses dubbed the "GC Surfer" will carry passengers south of Burleigh Heads, but without the dedicated lanes to bypass traffic.

The GC Surfer will also link the Gold Coast's inland suburbs, including Nerang and Robina, which would not have been feasible with light rail.

"Those communities sandwiched between light rail and heavy [rail] will now have the opportunity to enjoy both," Burleigh MP Hermann Vorster said.

An artist's impression has been released, but costs for the "GC Surfer" bus are yet to be finalised. (Supplied: Queensland Government)

Labor's only Gold Coast MP, Meaghan Scanlon, called the stage 3 launch without an airport extension "bittersweet" but stopped short of committing to stage 4.

With the city's population expected to reach one million in the next two decades, Mr Wales said the Gold Coast's "hesitation" towards public transport must change.

"If you look at any major city around the world, their mass transit is crucially important in terms of efficiency and economic development," he said.

"For us to be more prosperous, light rail is part of the solution."

World.title: NFL star uses Hall of Fame speech to announce he has dementia
World.content:
Former star NFL running back Roger Craig has revealed during his induction speech into the Pro Football Hall of Fame that he has vascular dementia.

The former San Francisco 49ers player spoke in a pre-recorded video message while he sat on stage wearing his gold jacket at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium in Canton, Ohio.

Presented by former teammate Jamie Williams, he received a standing ovation from the crowd and hugs from the many Hall of Famers on stage.

Nearly eight minutes into a nine-minute speech, Craig announced his diagnosis, saying his doctors believe "it may be related, at least in part, to the concussions" he experienced during his playing career.

"The changes were gradual," Craig said.

"At first, they were easy to dismiss as normal aging. Over time, my family noticed, too."

Symptoms of vascular dementia, according to the Mayo Clinic, include confusion; trouble finding the right words; difficulty paying attention; trouble organising thoughts or actions; difficulty planning and following through with plans; slowed thinking; uncertainty about what to do next; and memory issues.

Roger Craig was a trailblazer at the running back position for the San Francisco 49ers. (Getty Images: George Rose)

"Two things could be true," Craig said.

"Football gave me opportunities beyond anything I can imagine. It helped shape the man I became.

"At the same time, we know more today about brain health than when I played. I hope sharing my story encourages people to pay attention to their health and seek help when something doesn't feel right.

"I want people to know that this diagnosis doesn't define me. I am still Roger Craig. I am still a father, still a husband, a teammate, a friend and someone who loves this game and the people who brought it to my life.

Inside a brain with suspected CTE The effect of head knocks over Gordi Kirkbank-Ellis's decades-long sporting career isn't immediately obvious. That is, until you see what's happening to his brain.

"If sharing my story helps even one family or one former player, then it's worth it. Football gave me everything: opportunity, discipline, lifelong friends and the platform to grow as a man. This honour belongs to my parents who started it all."

Selected by the 49ers in the second round of the 1983 draft as a fullback out of Nebraska, Craig become one of the most versatile players in league history.

He excelled as a runner, receiver and blocker, helping the 49ers win three of their five Super Bowls.

In 1985, Craig became the first player in NFL history to have 1,000 yards rushing and 1,000 yards receiving in a season.

Craig was selected from the seniors category and entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2026 with Drew Brees, Larry Fitzgerald, Luke Kuechly and Adam Vinatieri.

World.title: Exhausted Vollering reclaims yellow jersey with one stage remaining
World.content:
Demi Vollering launched a blistering attack to win the eighth stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the yellow jersey heading into tonight's final stage.

The Dutchwoman upped the pace on the fourth and final small climb and title rival Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney cracked with about 6km to go, sitting back down in her saddle as 2023 Tour winner Vollering surged ahead.

As Vollering zoomed along the famed Promenade des Anglais by the seaside in Nice, Niewiadoma-Phinney and former Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini could not close the gap.

Demi Vollering collapses to the ground in a ice vest after a gruelling stage. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"It's funny but only this morning I saw myself taking the yellow jersey," Vollering said.

"I thought it might come true, that maybe that's the way things should be. During the day, I tried to remind myself I could do it."

So it proved.

Vollering raised her arms in triumph at the line, then collapsed to the ground and panted heavily as she tried to get her breath back.

"I was in so much pain, I can hardly describe it, but I made it happen," Vollering said.

"This goes to prove that if you really believe in something, if you dream big, it doesn't matter how much risk you take or how much pain you have to go through."

Longo Borghini was second and Niewiadoma-Phinney was third, both 17 seconds behind. The day belonged to Vollering, who won the Giro d'Italia this year to complete the hat-trick of Grands Tour wins.

She is eight seconds ahead of Niewiadoma-Phinney, the 2024 champion, in the overall standings. The Polish rider took the yellow jersey with a brilliant solo win up Mont Ventoux a day earlier, and rode a yellow bike to go with it on Stage 8.

The 172km route from Sisteron to Nice on the south-east coast was mostly flat for sprinters but featured four minor climbs which made it a little more tricky.

With the main title contenders initially saving energy for tonight's tough-looking decisive stage in the hills around Nice, the yellow jersey group let Frenchwoman Maeva Squiban and Dutchwoman Loes Adegeest form a long breakaway.

Squiban slid off her bike heading into a turn on a downhill section and landed heavily on her left side. She had cuts and grazes and screamed in agony as a medic on a motorbike tried bandaging her arm while she was riding.

She carried on riding despite the pain while, up ahead, Adegeest was caught inside the last 9km.

Defending champion withdraws

Pauline Ferrand-Prévôt pulled out of the race shortly before the stage after feeling unwell.

The French rider's Visma-Lease a Bike team said on X that the decision to pull her out of the race was made after consultation with the team's medical staff.

Why broadcasting row has Tour de France Femmes fans 'pissed off' In the Tour de France Femmes, less than 40 seconds separates the top three riders with only two stages to go. That's just one reason why supporters are questioning why they can't watch the entire race.

The 2024 Paris Olympic champion in mountain biking won the Tour de France Femmes on her debut last year. But she struggled this year and was in 14th place overall before withdrawing.

The final stage tonight features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, which is nestled in the hills overlooking the tiny Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on a final day mountain stage to win the race by just four seconds.

Vollering will have to ensure it is not a case of déjà vu.

"Tomorrow's course is going to be super hard," she said.

"We knew it from the beginning of the Tour."

World.title: Win City2Surf, turn around, run 14km back: a champion’s Sunday schedule
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWCity to Surf Win City2Surf, turn around, run 14km back: a champion’s Sunday schedule Patrick Begley August 9, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After tasting victory in this year’s 14-kilometre City2Surf race, Andy Buchanan said he planned to change shoes and “run back to the start”. He has marathons to train for, after all. More than 90,000 people are taking part in this year’s City2Surf. Oscar Colman The 35-year-old Victorian, who held the Australian marathon record, crossed the line first in a field of about 90,000 participants, with a time of 40 minutes and 27 seconds. The course record of 40:03, set by Olympian Steve Moneghetti in 1991, grew a year older.



“I missed it by a fair bit this year, but I’ll be back to try to get it,” said Buchanan, who represented Australia in the marathon at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. Related Article City to Surf Meet the Babblers: The City2Surf’s most talkative squad Holly Campbell took out the women’s race, crossing the line at Bondi in 46:35. Competing in the elite category of the race for the first time, the 30-year-old surpassed the time her twin sister Paige set when she came second two years ago. “I dreamed about winning this race as a kid,” Campbell, who grew up on a farm in central NSW, said. “Dreams do come true.” Not everyone was taking the world’s biggest fun run so seriously.



A group of four runners dressed as football referees and linesmen were “just keeping everyone in check”, with a whistle and a red card in the pocket. Not chickening out: City2Surf participants making their way toward Bondi. Oscar Colman Many more wore costumes, for a laugh or for charity. Participants have raised more than $63 million for good causes since the fundraising total was first recorded in 2008. The race began at 7.30am, but before dawn contestants had begun to gather at the start line near Hyde Park in the CBD. Diego Soto, wearing blue-tinted aviator sunglasses, was hoping for a time below an hour. His strategy was “run fast before Heartbreak Hill”, the steep stretch between Rose Bay and Vaucluse.



Another early riser, Dan Agnew, said “everybody complains about it” but he liked Heartbreak Hill. “It’s actually really cool,” said Agnew, who was also hoping for a sub-60 minute time. Jessy Bonney’s pre-race preparation included listening to “upbeat emo music” as she readied herself to draw on the crowd’s momentum. “You feel everybody’s energy for the ‘ready, set, go’, you just use it,” Bonney said. “You’re part of that bubble.” Omid Toloo said he has run the race since 1996. Oscar Colman Personal trainer Omid Toloo said this year’s City2Surf would be his 31st and he hoped there would be many more to come. “If I last until I’m 80, I’m happy.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. World.title: Two planes involved in near-miss while taxiing at Sydney Airport
World.content:
Two planes have been involved in a near-miss while taxiing on the runway at Sydney Airport, forcing one plane to brake suddenly and injuring a crew member.

A Qatar Airways plane and a Jetstar plane were photographed on the runway metres from each other just after 7am on Sunday.

A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News

There were 180 passengers on board Jetstar flight JQ402, which was heading to the Gold Coast, when the pilot spotted a Qatar Boeing 777 aircraft next to the plane, Nine News reported. The Qatar plane did not have any passengers on board and was being towed at the time, according to the report.

The pilot applied the brakes on the Airbus A320, causing one flight attendant who was moving throughout the cabin to fall. The attendant was treated by paramedics for minor injuries. No passengers were injured.

World.title: Skinny is the new skinny: how body extremes reflect the zeitgeist
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Opinion Skinny is the new skinny: how body extremes reflect the zeitgeist Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist August 9, 2026 — 9:30am

August 9, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has proven himself incapable, so far, of winning the unnecessary Iran war he started with his president, Donald Trump. So when he announced last month that he was going to be testing all “war fighters” in the US military for their testosterone levels, it was tempting to believe Hegseth was projecting, to use the psychological term for when someone attributes their own weaknesses to another person. Ariana Grande’s video for her song Petal has led to comments about her weight. YouTube “Under the supervision of our world-class medical professionals, war fighters age 30 and older are going to be tested annually as part of their periodic health assessment,” Hegseth said in a video posted to X, titled “The High-T Department of War”. Addressing his troops, but only the male ones, it seems, he said the military needs to “constantly look for new ways to optimise your performance … ensuring you have the right testosterone levels to operate at your absolute best”.



He said troops with low testosterone levels would be topped up with hormone replacement therapy, to restore their “natural” function. I’m no expert in military strategy, but even setting aside what such a pronouncement might do for the morale of your personnel, it seems strange to signal to your enemies that your troops might not be man enough. It also sends a strong exclusionary signal to all women in the US military, from the same man who has blocked the recommended promotions of high-ranking women and people of colour, to a disproportionate degree. As the United States polarises ever further politically, it seems the extremism in politics is jumping the fence and moving into other areas of public life – notably gender politics and the way men and women present themselves physically. As men are encouraged to looksmaxx and take peptides to get larger and more imposing, to drive their muscles into hard edges and plane their chins to strong, manly angles, women are shrinking.



The extreme of the late-noughties body positivity movement, where some unhealthy bodies were presented as celebratory and desirable, has now swung to the other end of the pendulum. “Clavicular” is the physical ideal of young men who are “looksmaxxing”. Aresna Villanueva A new kind of (possibly peptide-charged) thinness is now normal and increasingly common. We see it on red carpets and in movies and on all the celebrity Instagram accounts, usually attributed to a Pilates regime and plenty of green juice. This week, the pop star Ariana Grande drew widespread attention when she released a music video for her new song “Petal” in which she looks skeletal, the bones of her shoulders protruding like those of a famine-struck child.



Grande has shrunk herself into cartoonishly tiny proportions, and yet, the narrative of the film clip depicts a jobbing actress being repeatedly rejected by a panel of ugly studio-exec men for being “not good enough”. The video ends with Grande, in character, returning to the audition room with a chainsaw and hacking the men to bloody pieces. One minute she is cloyingly seeking their approval, the next she is massacring them: talk about extremes. Fans have taken to social media to express concern about Grande’s gaunt appearance, and it has sparked multiple think-pieces on Substack and in major newspapers about whether it’s okay to comment on women’s bodies, even when it’s under the guise of worrying about their health. Grande has this week released a statement saying she will be “taking a step back from visibility”.



It is perhaps a small consolation that men now subject themselves to this sort of body scrutiny, and they are subjected to it in the media, too. This week The Times of London published an article about the “mini-paunch” of newly anointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The article noted that Burnham is “slim and fit” and has competed in various marathons. But “despite his efforts the new PM has found attention directed to his barely there mini-paunch, somewhat unfairly dubbed the ‘Burnham belly’”. But the tone of the article was interesting – rather than fat-shaming Burnham, his problem paunch was framed as something that can happen to even the healthiest of men, and nothing terribly serious to worry about.



Related Article Opinion

Eating disorders Is it OK to mention how skinny female celebrities are getting? Again? Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist The writer shared various tips to get rid of male belly fat, if you really wanted to. By contrast, Burnham’s wife, Marie-France Van Heel, was widely critiqued online for wearing a baby blue Victoria Beckham midi-dress on her first official outing with her husband. I thought she looked great, but internet trolls did what they do to women who aren’t within the boundaries of whatever they decree is acceptable. The casual fat-shaming of a prime ministerial wife and the skinny-shaming of a famous pop star are probably two sides of the same coin; two extremes of the same sickness.



Of course, in the United States, no social phenomenon pops up without many entrepreneurs popping up to monetise it. The new crop of “skinny influencers” are remarkably different from diet-peddlers of the past. Instagram So it is with the new thinness. The new crop of “skinny influencers” – who collectively have millions of followers, and subscriber-only clubs where women can join chat groups and see exclusive “skinny” content – are remarkably different from diet-peddlers past. Their central message is to “drop the rules” many yo-yo dieters have had around food, and to develop a “normal” relationship with it, eating everything, but just not too much of it. One such influencer recently posted about how she had been craving a cinnamon scroll. So she ordered one on Uber Eats, ate a small portion of it and then threw it away.



This influencer purports to be selling self-composure, regulation and healthy control. The skinny influencers evangelise that they can take or leave food, having a bite and then setting it down, and they claim that they can teach others this skill. The irony of creating a career around decentring food, while constantly talking about, well, food, is lost on them. Since humans were able to make images of themselves and others, certain standards of appearance have been elevated above others. Artists and romantics have always sought an ideal of beauty, and from the foot-binding of Ming Dynasty China to the corsetry of Victorian England, that ideal has often necessitated the suffering of women. But the current crop of skinny influencers are not peddling beauty, per se. They are peddling control and perhaps the related ideal of “hotness”, and it’s now spread to men who risk becoming just as strictured-by-expectation as women.



They are selling an extreme, which is the ultimate zeitgeist product. Jacqueline Maley is an author and columnist. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Iran makes dramatic new demands around Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Iran makes dramatic new demands around Strait of Hormuz August 9, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Iran issued dramatic new demands around the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile. Yemen’s military attacked the country’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. Here’s a look at developments across the Middle East. People spend time at a beach as commercial vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran. AP Photo/Amirhosein Khorgooi Iran says the strait won’t open until the US ‘corrects’ its behaviour Iran’s politburo-like body known as the Supreme National Security Council said the Strait of Hormuz would not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, issuing new demands that could shake up talks on a deal to manage the waterway.



Iran’s state broadcaster published the statement by the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the powerful Revolutionary Guard. Related Article Middle East at war Eight backflips and counting: Trump is still promising his big Iran ‘deal’ The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets. There was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal first on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and plan on compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets. A 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended.



Iran has said it is close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said they were close to reaching an agreement on navigation, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening was contingent on other conditions, he said in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal. Loading Oman, a mediator Gulf Arab country that has said relatively little on the talks, said in a statement that the discussions were ongoing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait. The strait, crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low.



Iran attacks a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, the UAE says A vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned ADNOC oil and gas company was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said. The Foreign Ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping. Related Article Middle East at war State Department warns US citizens to be ready to leave Middle East as Iran tensions boil ADNOC said in a statement there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday (Tehran time). The company said more than a dozen of its vessels had been attacked by missiles and drones while transiting the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member had been killed and 20 others wounded, it said. ADNOC didn’t elaborate on the attack’s location or any damage.



Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman, had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, with the vessel and crew safe. It was not clear whether this was the ADNOC incident. Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy Trump’s ‘short war’ is spiralling out of control. His personal failings were the trigger Rodger Shanahan Middle East and security analyst A defence deal is not aimed at any third country, Turkey says A defence agreement that Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed on Friday was not aimed against any third country, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said. It says an attack on one would be considered an attack on all three. Fidan told Turkey’s state-run Anadolu Agency that the countries did not view any state as an adversary unless it took hostile action against them: “We don’t have anything written down – nothing we’ve signed – that defines a common threat.”



Asked how the mutual defence mechanism would work, Fidan said a member would formally request help and the two countries’ assistance could range from intelligence-sharing to logistics support or the deployment of military units. The mechanism would establish a secretariat to be based in Saudi Arabia, Fidan said. He said other nations, which he did not name, had expressed interest in joining the agreement, adding that he expected Egypt, which he described as a “natural partner”, to participate “at the next stage”. Yemen’s military attacks Iran-backed Houthis The attacks were in response to the Houthis’ recent strikes in central and eastern Yemen. Colonel Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for Yemen’s military, said the attacks targeted the rebels’ “sites and capabilities” on multiple front lines, without elaborating. The escalation between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government and its backer, a Saudi-supported coalition, threatens to reignite Yemen’s civil war following a 2022 truce.

World.title: Labor wanted to restore Sydney’s nightlife. But young people don’t have ‘time for hangovers’
World.content:
In a grassy inner-west field, young Sydneysiders are making their own ‘nightlife’ one picnic blanket at a time.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On a cool Saturday afternoon, young Sydneysiders gently groove to an electronic jazz band performing on a makeshift stage of red Persian rugs in the middle of a grassy inner-west park. As the winter sunset’s golden haze descends over the free public gig, it washes over the very faces that have become the subject of discussion among dozens of MPs, hospitality and nightlife stakeholders on Macquarie Street. Over three hearings in May and June, an inquiry assessed the health of the state’s live music scene post-lockout laws, post-COVID and following the NSW government’s vibrancy reforms. Almost three years ago, those reforms aimed to reverse a decade’s worth of damage caused by the shutdown of the city’s nightlife in the wake of alcohol-fuelled violence in 2014. Young revellers sit on picnic blankets at a free public gig at Sydney Park. Audrey Richardson The brainchild of Music and Nighttime Economy Minister John Graham, the $150 million reforms have been rolled out in three tranches. Many have involved removing red tape, such as stripping councils’ noise complaint powers, overhauling planning departments to allow designated nightlife areas to operate later, and incentivising businesses to host live music. Budgeted at $54.4 million a year, the reforms have been popular – between March 2023 and 2025, there was a 320 per cent increase in venues accessing live music incentives, NSW government data shows. The most recent data from 2023 found that live music generated about $5.5 billion in economic output and added $2.7 billion in value to the NSW economy. However, the incentives, which allow venues and hotels to secure an extra two hours of trade and a liquor licensing discount in return for putting on live acts, have led to claims of musicians playing covers in the corner of “pokies pubs”.



And the reforms did not account for broader phenomena, such as the one taking place in Alexandria’s Sydney Park, in which cost-of-living pressures push gigs into the public domain, and generational gender, technological and political upheavals impact how young revellers party. “People are quite hungry to be in spaces that are different and things that are new and exciting,” says John Troughton (also known as Heartholder), the 28-year-old saxophonist and organiser of the Sydney Park gig. Younger people are also drinking less, says Adrian Farrugia, a researcher at La Trobe University’s Australian Research Centre in Sex, Health and Society. This trend has led to experimental and “third space” venues such as nighttime library events, as so-called traditional venues continue to close. “The notion of being young – and that being a time of living in the moment and being unruly and being a bit risky – that seems to have changed,” Farrugia says. “People are worried about the future.”



There’s another problem emerging from the Minns government reforms too. One that policymakers, revellers, industry lobbies, promoters, event organisers and venue owners are nervous to speak up about – the licensing police. The ‘well-entrenched’ policing culture NSW Greens MP Cate Faehrmann believes that the attitude of licensing police is a problem for both venues and revellers. Danny Rispler plays drums during the Sydney Park gig. Audrey Richardson “We’ve got this one part of government that’s throwing money at venues and precincts, and encouraging people to go out and enjoy themselves,” Faehrmann says. “While the culture of the police is that anybody who goes out to enjoy themselves at night is fair game.” In June this year, police officers with drug detection dogs attended several Oxford Street nightlife venues – including popular LGBTQ nightclub Universal in Surry Hills – targeting drug supply and antisocial behaviour. The incidents prompted Sydney MP Alex Greenwich and Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore to ask the police watchdog to investigate allegations of aggression and heavy-handedness. During the first live music inquiry hearing, in May, Acting Assistant Commissioner Paul Dunstan provided evidence for NSW Police. In it, he said the force was committed to supporting nightlife, but conceded that work was still needed to reshape attitudes inside a “well-entrenched licensing policing community”.



“Most of them have been involved in the game for a very long time,” Dunstan told the inquiry. “We need to change some hearts and minds there to be more supportive. But I think, like any organisation, the tone is set from the top.” Dunstan revealed that less than a month into his role as police commissioner, Mal Lanyon affirmed his commitment to the vibrancy reforms at a forum established by 24-Hour Economy Commissioner Michael Rodrigues. But despite Rodrigues and his office meeting “the licensing police to try and speak and educate the police on where we’re heading”, according to Dunstan, the message has yet to trickle down through the organisation. “It’s a lot of communication through a hierarchical organisation,” Dunstan says. Faehrmann believes the licensing police’s approach has tarnished Sydney’s nightlife reputation and there’s a fear of openly criticising them. “A number of businesses and venue owners who speak to me will not go public because of fear of retaliation in terms of the police targeting their business,” she says.



Graham is aware of the issues raised by Faehrmann and the Oxford Street incident. “I was concerned to hear about these reports,” he says. John Troughton, aka Heartholder. Audrey Richardson “In Kings Cross we had a culture which got out of control [leading up to the lockout laws]. It was one culture in one place and one offering, often with one age group, and unsurprisingly, it didn’t work. Police were on the front line of that … things have definitely improved. We’ve still got more work to do in the relationship between venues and police.” Sydney Park gig organiser Troughton says the police presence at public events or unconventional locations has become less overbearing. “I’ve been to some recent events, raves in abandoned warehouses and buildings in not traditional locations, like Marrickville, like inner city ... the cops come through and see how well it’s run, and [they] sort of leave it alone,” Troughton says. People listening to Heartholder as he performs in Alexandria’s Sydney Park. Audrey Richardson The event the Herald attended was supposed to be the previous Saturday and had more than 850 people RSVP, Troughton says, but it was rescheduled due to rain. A few hundred joined the four-hour-long postponed party – a third of whom appeared to have stumbled upon it while walking through the park with their strollers, dogs and friends, drawn in by the ambient and electronic music.

World.title: Win City2Surf, turn around, run 14km back: a champion’s Sunday schedule
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWCity to Surf Win City2Surf, turn around, run 14km back: a champion’s Sunday schedule Patrick Begley August 9, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After tasting victory in this year’s 14-kilometre City2Surf race, Andy Buchanan said he planned to change shoes and “run back to the start”. He has marathons to train for, after all. More than 90,000 people are taking part in this year’s City2Surf. Oscar Colman The 35-year-old Victorian, who held the Australian marathon record, crossed the line first in a field of about 90,000 participants, with a time of 40 minutes and 27 seconds. The course record of 40:03, set by Olympian Steve Moneghetti in 1991, grew a year older.



“I missed it by a fair bit this year, but I’ll be back to try to get it,” said Buchanan, who represented Australia in the marathon at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. Related Article City to Surf Meet the Babblers: The City2Surf’s most talkative squad Holly Campbell took out the women’s race, crossing the line at Bondi in 46:35. Competing in the elite category of the race for the first time, the 30-year-old surpassed the time her twin sister Paige set when she came second two years ago. “I dreamed about winning this race as a kid,” Campbell, who grew up on a farm in central NSW, said. “Dreams do come true.” Not everyone was taking the world’s biggest fun run so seriously.



A group of four runners dressed as football referees and linesmen were “just keeping everyone in check”, with a whistle and a red card in the pocket. Not chickening out: City2Surf participants making their way towards Bondi. Oscar Colman Many more wore costumes, for a laugh or for charity. Participants have raised more than $63 million for good causes since the fundraising total was first recorded in 2008. The race began at 7.30am, but before dawn contestants had begun to gather at the start line near Hyde Park in the CBD. Diego Soto, wearing blue-tinted aviator sunglasses, was hoping for a time below an hour. His strategy was “run fast before Heartbreak Hill”, the steep stretch between Rose Bay and Vaucluse.



Another early riser, Dan Agnew, said “everybody complains about it” but he liked Heartbreak Hill. “It’s actually really cool,” said Agnew, who was also hoping for a sub-60 minute time. Jessy Bonney’s pre-race preparation included listening to “upbeat emo music” as she readied herself to draw on the crowd’s momentum. “You feel everybody’s energy for the ‘ready, set, go’, you just use it,” Bonney said. “You’re part of that bubble.” Omid Toloo said he has run the race since 1996. Oscar Colman Personal trainer Omid Toloo said this year’s City2Surf would be his 31st and he hoped there would be many more to come. “If I last until I’m 80, I’m happy.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. World.title: Two planes involved in near-miss while taxiing at Sydney Airport
World.content:
Two planes have been involved in a near-miss while taxiing on the runway at Sydney Airport, forcing one plane to brake suddenly and injuring a crew member.

A Qatar Airways plane and a Jetstar plane were photographed on the runway metres from each other just after 7am on Sunday.

A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News

There were 180 passengers on board Jetstar flight JQ402, which was heading to the Gold Coast, when the pilot spotted a Qatar Boeing 777 aircraft next to the plane, Nine News reported. The Qatar plane did not have any passengers on board and was being towed at the time, according to the report.

The pilot applied the brakes on the Airbus A320, causing one flight attendant who was moving throughout the cabin to fall. The attendant was treated by paramedics for minor injuries. No passengers were injured.

World.title: Skinny is the new skinny: how body extremes reflect the zeitgeist
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Opinion Skinny is the new skinny: how body extremes reflect the zeitgeist Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist August 9, 2026 — 9:30am

August 9, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has proven himself incapable, so far, of winning the unnecessary Iran war he started with his president, Donald Trump. So when he announced last month that he was going to be testing all “war fighters” in the US military for their testosterone levels, it was tempting to believe Hegseth was projecting, to use the psychological term for when someone attributes their own weaknesses to another person. Ariana Grande’s video for her song Petal has led to comments about her weight. YouTube “Under the supervision of our world-class medical professionals, war fighters age 30 and older are going to be tested annually as part of their periodic health assessment,” Hegseth said in a video posted to X, titled “The High-T Department of War”. Addressing his troops, but only the male ones, it seems, he said the military needs to “constantly look for new ways to optimise your performance … ensuring you have the right testosterone levels to operate at your absolute best”.



He said troops with low testosterone levels would be topped up with hormone replacement therapy, to restore their “natural” function. I’m no expert in military strategy, but even setting aside what such a pronouncement might do for the morale of your personnel, it seems strange to signal to your enemies that your troops might not be man enough. It also sends a strong exclusionary signal to all women in the US military, from the same man who has blocked the recommended promotions of high-ranking women and people of colour, to a disproportionate degree. As the United States polarises ever further politically, it seems the extremism in politics is jumping the fence and moving into other areas of public life – notably gender politics and the way men and women present themselves physically. As men are encouraged to looksmaxx and take peptides to get larger and more imposing, to drive their muscles into hard edges and plane their chins to strong, manly angles, women are shrinking.



The extreme of the late-noughties body positivity movement, where some unhealthy bodies were presented as celebratory and desirable, has now swung to the other end of the pendulum. “Clavicular” is the physical ideal of young men who are “looksmaxxing”. Aresna Villanueva A new kind of (possibly peptide-charged) thinness is now normal and increasingly common. We see it on red carpets and in movies and on all the celebrity Instagram accounts, usually attributed to a Pilates regime and plenty of green juice. This week, the pop star Ariana Grande drew widespread attention when she released a music video for her new song “Petal” in which she looks skeletal, the bones of her shoulders protruding like those of a famine-struck child.



Grande has shrunk herself into cartoonishly tiny proportions, and yet, the narrative of the film clip depicts a jobbing actress being repeatedly rejected by a panel of ugly studio-exec men for being “not good enough”. The video ends with Grande, in character, returning to the audition room with a chainsaw and hacking the men to bloody pieces. One minute she is cloyingly seeking their approval, the next she is massacring them: talk about extremes. Fans have taken to social media to express concern about Grande’s gaunt appearance, and it has sparked multiple think-pieces on Substack and in major newspapers about whether it’s okay to comment on women’s bodies, even when it’s under the guise of worrying about their health. Grande has this week released a statement saying she will be “taking a step back from visibility”.



It is perhaps a small consolation that men now subject themselves to this sort of body scrutiny, and they are subjected to it in the media, too. This week The Times of London published an article about the “mini-paunch” of newly anointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The article noted that Burnham is “slim and fit” and has competed in various marathons. But “despite his efforts the new PM has found attention directed to his barely there mini-paunch, somewhat unfairly dubbed the ‘Burnham belly’”. But the tone of the article was interesting – rather than fat-shaming Burnham, his problem paunch was framed as something that can happen to even the healthiest of men, and nothing terribly serious to worry about.



Related Article Opinion

Eating disorders Is it OK to mention how skinny female celebrities are getting? Again? Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist The writer shared various tips to get rid of male belly fat, if you really wanted to. By contrast, Burnham’s wife, Marie-France Van Heel, was widely critiqued online for wearing a baby blue Victoria Beckham midi-dress on her first official outing with her husband. I thought she looked great, but internet trolls did what they do to women who aren’t within the boundaries of whatever they decree is acceptable. The casual fat-shaming of a prime ministerial wife and the skinny-shaming of a famous pop star are probably two sides of the same coin; two extremes of the same sickness.



Of course, in the United States, no social phenomenon pops up without many entrepreneurs popping up to monetise it. The new crop of “skinny influencers” are remarkably different from diet-peddlers of the past. Instagram So it is with the new thinness. The new crop of “skinny influencers” – who collectively have millions of followers, and subscriber-only clubs where women can join chat groups and see exclusive “skinny” content – are remarkably different from diet-peddlers past. Their central message is to “drop the rules” many yo-yo dieters have had around food, and to develop a “normal” relationship with it, eating everything, but just not too much of it. One such influencer recently posted about how she had been craving a cinnamon scroll. So she ordered one on Uber Eats, ate a small portion of it and then threw it away.



This influencer purports to be selling self-composure, regulation and healthy control. The skinny influencers evangelise that they can take or leave food, having a bite and then setting it down, and they claim that they can teach others this skill. The irony of creating a career around decentring food, while constantly talking about, well, food, is lost on them. Since humans were able to make images of themselves and others, certain standards of appearance have been elevated above others. Artists and romantics have always sought an ideal of beauty, and from the foot-binding of Ming Dynasty China to the corsetry of Victorian England, that ideal has often necessitated the suffering of women. But the current crop of skinny influencers are not peddling beauty, per se. They are peddling control and perhaps the related ideal of “hotness”, and it’s now spread to men who risk becoming just as strictured-by-expectation as women.



They are selling an extreme, which is the ultimate zeitgeist product. Jacqueline Maley is an author and columnist. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Iran makes dramatic new demands around Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Iran makes dramatic new demands around Strait of Hormuz August 9, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Iran issued dramatic new demands around the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile. Yemen’s military attacked the country’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. Here’s a look at developments across the Middle East. People spend time at a beach as commercial vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran. AP Photo/Amirhosein Khorgooi Iran says the strait won’t open until the US ‘corrects’ its behaviour Iran’s politburo-like body known as the Supreme National Security Council said the Strait of Hormuz would not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, issuing new demands that could shake up talks on a deal to manage the waterway.



Iran’s state broadcaster published the statement by the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the powerful Revolutionary Guard. Related Article Middle East at war Eight backflips and counting: Trump is still promising his big Iran ‘deal’ The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets. There was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal first on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and plan on compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets. A 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended.



Iran has said it is close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said they were close to reaching an agreement on navigation, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening was contingent on other conditions, he said in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal. Loading Oman, a mediator Gulf Arab country that has said relatively little on the talks, said in a statement that the discussions were ongoing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait. The strait, crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low.



Iran attacks a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, the UAE says A vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned ADNOC oil and gas company was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said. The Foreign Ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping. Related Article Middle East at war State Department warns US citizens to be ready to leave Middle East as Iran tensions boil ADNOC said in a statement there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday (Tehran time). The company said more than a dozen of its vessels had been attacked by missiles and drones while transiting the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member had been killed and 20 others wounded, it said. ADNOC didn’t elaborate on the attack’s location or any damage.



Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman, had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, with the vessel and crew safe. It was not clear whether this was the ADNOC incident. Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy Trump’s ‘short war’ is spiralling out of control. His personal failings were the trigger Rodger Shanahan Middle East and security analyst A defence deal is not aimed at any third country, Turkey says A defence agreement that Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed on Friday was not aimed against any third country, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said. It says an attack on one would be considered an attack on all three. Fidan told Turkey’s state-run Anadolu Agency that the countries did not view any state as an adversary unless it took hostile action against them: “We don’t have anything written down – nothing we’ve signed – that defines a common threat.”



Asked how the mutual defence mechanism would work, Fidan said a member would formally request help and the two countries’ assistance could range from intelligence-sharing to logistics support or the deployment of military units. The mechanism would establish a secretariat to be based in Saudi Arabia, Fidan said. He said other nations, which he did not name, had expressed interest in joining the agreement, adding that he expected Egypt, which he described as a “natural partner”, to participate “at the next stage”. Yemen’s military attacks Iran-backed Houthis The attacks were in response to the Houthis’ recent strikes in central and eastern Yemen. Colonel Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for Yemen’s military, said the attacks targeted the rebels’ “sites and capabilities” on multiple front lines, without elaborating. The escalation between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government and its backer, a Saudi-supported coalition, threatens to reignite Yemen’s civil war following a 2022 truce.

Washington: Former US president Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread beyond his bones and is very painful, his son, Hunter Biden, said in an interview with the BBC.

“The cancer has spread, metastasised into his bones and further,” Hunter Biden told BBC’s Newsnight, according to video posted online. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”

Joe Biden’s physical health and mental acuity drew scrutiny during his 2021 to 2025 presidency. AP Photo/Evan Vucci

A spokesman for the 83-year-old Democrat declined on Saturday (Washington time) to comment on Hunter Biden’s interview.

Biden revealed in May 2025, less than four months after he left the White House, that he had been diagnosed with an “aggressive form” of prostate cancer, saying at the time that it had spread to his bones.

A hiker who fell from Mount Beerwah on Saturday afternoon has spent the night stranded on the mountain, with a rescue operation under way to retrieve him.

Emergency services were called after the man, in his 20s, fell while hiking the popular Sunshine Coast Hinterland summit in the Glass House Mountains National Park about 4.30pm on Saturday.

The man suffered ankle injuries in the fall and was unable to descend the mountain.

Mount Beerwah is the highest of the Glass House Mountains and considered difficult to climb. Mehdi Rez/Google Maps

Paramedics and fire crews gathered at the base of Mount Beerwah, but due to the time of day and terrain, were unable to rescue him on Saturday.

World.title: National promises Budget Responsibility Rules if elected
World.content:
The National Party are calling on Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori to release their plans to get New Zealand back into surplus.

The party have commit to three so-called Budget Responsibility Rules aimed at returning to surplus, cutting debt and keeping taxes low, and promise to adhere to them if re-elected as a bulwark against economic shocks.

National leader Christoper Luxon said an economy that cannot support itself was both a financial and strategic risk.

"If the Crown's own books aren't in order, the whole country stays exposed and vulnerable to major shocks here at home and abroad."

Luxon said government have historically carried less debt than other developed countries as a buffer against crises, but that buffer had " eroded considerably."

"Rebuilding it is what allows a future government of whatever colour to meet the next earthquake, the next pandemic, the next global disruption without a fiscal crisis on top of the actual crisis it has to deal with." he said.

The Budget Responsibility Rules

Prioritising a return to surplus in 2028/29 and staying in surplus over time so the country's debt curve bends down

Getting debt down below 40 percent of GDP and keeping it there over time

Keeping taxes low by cutting Crown expenditure as a share of the economy down towards 30 percent of GDP

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said those rules were the "fiscal guard-rails" her party intended to follow, and it "well past time" for parties to set out their own.

"I accept the premise that says they are not yet in a position to provide a detailed fiscal plan, however, they should be well able to say whether they will commit to these three basic things that have informed the fiscal strategies of successive governments and which represents what it is to be a responsible fiscal manager." she said.

Willis said it was "striking" to her that Labour and the Greens set out their own fiscal rules leading up to the 2017 election but had not yet released theirs.

"As I stand here today I am not even aware whether they believe a surplus target is appropriate where they think debt should be or whether or not they believe that we need to reduce core crown spending in order to keep taxes low. "

"Those are very basic questions and they do form the parameters for National's campaign."

Asked if National would commit to not imposing next taxes if elected, Willis said there would be "no new taxes on working people".

Pushed again, she said the party's tax policies would be released over the course of the election.

"Listen to me very carefully, no new taxes on working people... what New Zealanders can expect is no new taxes on their work, their savings, their investments or their capital." she said.

Budget 2026 forecasted a return to a budget surplus in 2028/29 from a mix of an increased tax take, controls on government spending, capital projects and a reduction in borrowing and debt service costs.

Three years too late - ACT's Seymour

ACT leader David Seymour said National's promise to follow the rules was three years too late.

In a statement, Seymour said saving money took courage.

"Reducing spending to 30 percent of GDP sounds impressive, but Grant Robertson spent only 28 percent in his first two budgets before he lost all control during Covid. Today the government is spending 32.6 percent of GDP and isn't forecast to go below 30 this decade.

"Achieving 30 percent of GDP will take real courage to face down the causes of higher spending. They are rising superannuation and health costs, rising welfare costs, and the size and complexity of cabinet and government departments."

Seymour said his party had a track record of taking on hard issues, pointing to changes to pay equity and the school lunch programme.

"National wanted to spend $380 [million] on a medical school, we negotiated it down to $80 million. They wanted to spend $250 million on electric car chargers, we got it down to a repayable loan of $60 million. National wanted to pay out $375 million in tax credits for fuel, even if the price went back down.

"ACT may still save the taxpayer hundreds of millions more with the sensible suggestion that the payments end when fuel prices normalise."

He said ACT "killed" three new taxes while in government.

"Without ACT we would be seeing taxes on housing, tourism and banks that are all ultimately paid by New Zealanders and their businesses. Controlling spending is only half the equation, controlling taxes is the other half ... the taxpayer would be on the hook for billions more, but even more savings are needed." he said.

Rules silly and meaningless - Greens' Swarbrick

Green Party co-leader Chloe Swarbrick told RNZ the rules were silly and meaningless.

"If all it takes for you to meet your goals is to set goals or KPIs that are completely untethered from improving people's lives, then sure, well done, you're hitting your bingo card," she said.

"But people's lives aren't getting any better, and I think that makes you a pretty bloody irresponsible government."

Swarbrick said the rules could stand in the way of critical infrastructure investment.

"If you're just fixated on the headline figures without any meaningful investigation or interrogation of what it is that we're using this debt or this spending for, where the revenue is actually coming from for the government, how equitable that actually is, then ultimately we're kind of having a meaningless conversation."

World.title: 80% of road travel out of Wellington wouldn't be possible after 7.5 magnitude quake - study
World.content:
A study simulating what would happen to Wellington's road network in a major earthquake has found some parts would be cut off for months.

The simulation, published in the International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction, assessed the disruption that would be caused by a 7.5 magnitude quake on the Wellington Fault.

The researchers referenced a 2011 study that estimated a 10 percent chance such an earthquake would strike in the next 100 years.

They simulated traffic using parameters like driver reaction time and jam density then applied it to a map of the North Island based on a previous study assessing the infrastructure damage caused by such an earthquake.

On the map, several key roads had been closed including multiple stretches of State Highway 1, Hutt Road, Grant Road, Curtis Street and Chaytor Street.

In the immediate three-day aftermath, the researchers found 68 percent of trips into the Wellington region and 82 percent of trips out of Wellington would be infeasible.

After three months, that reduced to 25 percent of trips into Wellington and 49 percent of trips out of Wellington.

They found Lower Hutt, followed by Wellington City, would be most impacted.

Researchers also found successful trips were much slower, with simulated traffic spreading onto urban detour routes which increased travel times.

But the researchers acknowledged the simulation was limited by assuming demand for travel would remain steady, while in reality many motorists would baulk at the travel time and decide not to drive.

"While this assumption enabled stress-testing of network performance under disruption, it may overestimate congestion and trip cancellations by not accounting for behavioural adaptation during recovery," the paper said.

The researchers said the results highlighted the importance of spending on critical roads to ensure they stayed resilient.

World.title: Tankers, toilets on Ohakune streets after water pipe breaks
World.content:
A water tanker and portable toilets are being installed around the central North Island town of Ohakune as water supplies come under threat.

The Ruapehu District Council said the recent 5.9 earthquake near Taumarunui had caused a major break in the buried raw water pipeline supplying the treatment plant.

Residents and visitors are being asked to conserve supplies.

A water tanker is outside the council office on Ayr Street for people who bring their own containers.

Five-litre bottles of drinking water and portable toilets have also been distributed around the town.

World.title: Person in critical condition after stabbing in Central Auckland
World.content:
One person is in hospital with serious injuries after an alleged stabbing in Central Auckland overnight.

Emergency services were called to Karangahape Road near Pitt Street at 4:20am.

A Hato Hone St John spokesperson said ambulance crews assessed and treated one patient who was transported to Auckland City hospital in a critical condition.

One person underwent surgery and remains in hospital in a stable condition.

Two people have been arrested.

Detective senior sergeant Greg Brand said the person underwent surgery and was now in a stable condition.

He confirmed that two people had been arrested.

World.title: Warnings issued as heavy rain heads to Bay of Plenty, Northland
World.content:
MetService is forecasting heavy rain for Northland and eastern Bay of Plenty as a front moves eastward across northern and central North Island on Sunday and early Monday.

An orange rain warning is in place for the ranges of eastern Bay of Plenty. MetService forecasts 70 to 90mm of rain, peaking at 10 to 20mm/h expected. The warning is for 12 hours from 3pm Sunday to 3am Monday.

It warned that streams and rivers may rise rapidly, and that surface flooding, slips and difficult driving conditions were possible. Avoid low-lying areas and drive cautiously, it said.

There was minimal chance of the warning being upgraded to red.

A yellow rain watch is in place for the north and east of Northland. MetService forecasts periods of heavy rain that may approach warning levels.

There was a low risk of localised downpours that could briefly boost rainfall rates to 25 to 40mm/h, it said, and a moderate chance of upgrading to a warning. The watch is until 8pm Sunday.

World.title: Mistake to omit creative arts technologies from new school subjects, drama teachers say
World.content:
*This story has been updated to clarify comments made by Annette Thomson.

The drama teachers' association says the government has made a mistake by omitting technologies that support the creative arts from its list of new industry-led school subjects.

The nine subjects would be developed by industry skills boards to provide clear pathways to further training and jobs for secondary school students in Years 12-13.

Whakaari Aotearoa Drama New Zealand said it should have included a subject that covered areas like lighting, sound, staging, costume, and set design.

The organisation's president Annette Thomson said failing to do so would sever students' pathway into industries such as film and television that had critical skill shortages.

Whakaari Aotearoa Drama president Annette Thomson. Supplied / Whakaari Aotearoa Drama NZ

She said currently teens could earn credits toward an NCEA qualification in areas like lighting or sound, but that would not be possible under the new qualification being introduced in 2029 because students would have to study entire subjects and there was no subject that covered those skills.

Thomson said the decision endangered the government's plan to grow the creative sector's economic contribution to $22 billion a year by 2030.

"We feel like they're not really thinking about some of these things that are actually important. They do actively contribute to GDP and to our students," she said.

"All we're seeing is a cutting, a reducing, a narrowing of subjects in the arts."

World.title: Mt Eden prisoner sent to hospital after injuring themselves
World.content:
A prisoner from the Mt Eden Corrections Facility was taken to hospital on Saturday evening.

A corrections spokesperson said the prisoner appeared to have injured themselves.

The spokesperson said the prisoner was in a single cell.

They were unable to provide further information on the prisoner's condition and treatment.

World.title: Hamilton armed robbers found sleeping on mattress in garage after targeting Four Square for vapes
World.content:
As three people armed with weapons and wearing hoods ran into a Four Square supermarket, jumping the front counter, a staff member wondered what the noise was.

Coming out of the kitchen, she walked towards the till and was confronted by Jayden Bint, 24, and his two co-offenders, holding either tyre irons or hedge clippers.

One of them approached her and hit the door to the kitchen with a tyre iron, scaring her and causing her to lock herself inside the kitchen.

Bint's co-offender, meanwhile, stripped the cupboards of vape products and cigarette lighters and handed them to him.

Bint recently appeared in the Hamilton District Court for sentencing on charges of aggravated robbery, motor vehicle conversion, theft of a motor vehicle, breaching release conditions, and two charges of failing to attend court.

Court documents state that two cars were stolen from around Hamilton for the robbery - one from York St, the other from Silverdale Rd - during Waitangi weekend this year.

At 7.27am on 6 February, Bint and two others arrived at the Four Square in Cambridge in a white Toyota Aqua.

Two staff members were working; one was stacking shelves and the other was in the kitchen near the till.

The trio, all wearing disguises, ran in, with Bint's associates jumping over the counter.

After the staff member locked herself in the kitchen, the associates emptied the cigarette cupboard and passed the stolen items to Bint.

All three fled the store and drove to Epping Place in Hamilton, where they dumped the car.

They then jumped into the second car before dumping it in Rachel Place.

Police then received information that the trio had been seen entering a property in Duke St, Hamilton.

There, the defendants were found asleep on a mattress in a garage, two of them still wearing clothing matching that seen during the robbery.

A Nike backpack also contained some of the stolen lighters and vapes.

Addiction 'plainly entrenched'

Bint had earlier accepted a sentence indication from Judge Philip Crayton, who adopted an overall starting point of four years and seven months before applying discounts for Bint's guilty plea and youth.

The judge then took into account Bint's criminal history, which included violence and firearm offending.

He also noted Bint's drug addiction, which he said was "plainly entrenched" in that history.

"It is going to be important that you take steps to try and address that [addiction], otherwise you are just going to be back before the court getting longer and longer sentences."

Judge Crayton issued Bint a first strike under the Three Strikes legislation, and a firearms prohibition order, "due to the risk you pose to public safety".

He jailed Bint for two years and 11 months.

The co-offenders are being dealt with in the Youth Court on the matter.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Fijian rugby pro, 26, dies of suspected heat stroke after training
World.content:
Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi has died of suspected heat stroke after a training session in Japan. He was 26.

His death was announced on Saturday by his team, Kyushu Electric Power Kyuden Voltex — known as Kyushu KV.

The Japanese second-division club said Vunilagi died on Friday after falling ill on Monday and being hospitalised.

"After team practice on Monday … Saimoni displayed symptoms consistent with severe heat stroke," the team said in a statement Saturday.

"He was transported to a medical facility for treatment, but despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away."

Kyushu KV is based in Fukuoka, a city in southwestern Japan. Temperatures there reportedly reached around 35C on Monday.

"The players, staff, and all team associates are devastated by this sudden news," the team said.

Back rower Vunilagi joined Kyushu KV last month, having previously played in the Japanese top flight with Tokyo Sungoliath.

"Although Saimoni had only recently joined Kyushu KV, his generous spirit and powerful style of play had raised high hopes for his contributions in the upcoming season," Kyushu KV added.

"We humbly pray for the repose of his soul and extend our heartfelt condolences to his bereaved family."

The club supplied no other details surrounding the death.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
