World.title: 'I felt I wasn't worthy': Para athletes on barriers in elite sport
World.content:
At her debut Games in Paris, Nikki Ayers rowed herself into the record books, alongside Jed Altschwager, as the first Australians to win a gold medal in Para rowing.

Despite this success, the now 35-year-old, initially decided to take a break from rowing after the Games due to a difficult relationship with a member of her support team.

"[They] made me feel like I had less value, made me feel like I wasn't good enough," Ayers told ABC Sport.

"At times I felt objectified, that I wasn't worthy of being anything more than someone who could win a gold medal."

Nikki Ayers reached the pinnacle of her rowing career, alongside Jed Altschwager, at the 2024 Paralympics in Paris. (Getty: Naomi Baker)

Ayers, who was nervous to disclose her experiences, spent several months talking to ABC Sport before coming to a decision to retire from rowing completely.

Ayers is a partial leg amputee, is queer, and has experienced sexism and homophobia, alongside ableism.

"[I want] people to realise the impact that it has so we can create change to stop it from happening," she said.

"So, we can recognise women as the amazing [people] that we are and that we can contribute to society equally as well."

The bravery and strength Ayers has shown is immense.

"There just hasn't been the psychological safety for me at a level where I feel safe to pursue more within that sport," she said.

"It's not an easy decision, especially as an athlete."

Support from her teammate, Jed Altschwager, was important to Nikki Ayers on her Para rowing journey. (Getty: Adam Davy PA Images)

It is a strength that she shares with one of Australia's veteran Paralympians, Danni Di Toro.

Also, a proudly queer athlete, Di Toro has won 10 Australian Opens and competed in eight Paralympic Games across two sports.

But that strength comes not from a specific event, but from a sporting landscape dominated by male athletes, coaches and managers.

"It took me dealing with a lot of pretty average attitudes, that forced me to kind of be really firm," she told ABC Sport.

"If you're a female and you're going up against men in positions of power and you don't feel confident, then that is a very scary environment."

Danni Di Toro has competed in eight Paralympic Games across two sports, becoming a mentor to other athletes along the way. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Di Toro and Ayers aren't alone; their experiences have been shared by many disabled athletes, who responded to the ABC's Elite Athletes in Australian Women's Sport survey.

It found half of respondents who identified as living with a disability have experienced discrimination because of their impairment.

Having to choose between rent and eating

Despite some positive change across the Paralympic movement, there are still systemic issues that are holding many disabled athletes back from full participation in sport at all levels.

From inequity around prize money to athletes having to personally fund their entire sports career, female disabled athletes can end up leaving sport entirely or cutting their careers short.

Only in recent years have Paralympians, like Alexa Leary, been awarded medal incentive payments. (Getty: Sean M. Haffey)

For those competing in sports included in the Paralympics, funding can be more reliable, but there are still disparities.

Unlike Olympians, who have been receiving medal incentive payments since 2016, Paralympians have only received similar incentives since the Tokyo Games in 2021.

And while the Australian Olympic Committee fully funds these payments to Olympic medallists, Paralympics Australia, which is a charity, lacks the funds to cover similar payments to our Paralympians, with the federal government picking up the cost.

For athletes like Ayers, who is a trained nurse, receiving financial support from their National Sporting Organisation made the world of difference.

"For me to receive the financial support that I did from Rowing Australia, who do fund the Para athletes equally within the program, I was able to work less and focus more on training and work towards that goal," Ayers said.

Some sports equipment, like specialised wheelchairs for basketball, can cost athletes thousands of dollars. (Getty: James Fearn )

Ayers said the high cost of additional equipment, like racing wheelchairs and prosthetics, could also make competing more expensive for disabled athletes.

This specialist equipment can cost upwards of $30,000.

"That's where that financial gap can be quite vital and important for people with disabilities so they can stay in the sport, represent their country and go to the Paralympic Games," Ayres said.

Some athletes in the survey said if not for receiving some level of sponsorship they would have lost money, while others spoke of discrepancies in sponsorship opportunities, and many spoke about the lack of events to win prize money in.

"Even at local races, the 'elite' able-bodied athletes will often get prize money, whereas Para-athletes don't," one respondent said.

"In my sport, the males [both able and para] seem to get a lot more sponsorships than the females, even when we outperform them."

Di Toro acknowledged that she was one of the lucky ones, winning prize money when she was a wheelchair tennis player, but knew of many athletes who were having to choose between paying their rent or eating.

Danni Di Toro competed in wheelchair tennis at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, but now competes in wheelchair table tennis. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

"Funding is tricky, I often feel like there's a real disconnect between what we financially need to do to compete and what is actually being provided," she said.

"We prop these athletes up on these high pedestals, and we're so proud of them, and yet I don't think most Australians know what athletes are doing and how they're trying to actually make ends meet."

In a statement, the Australian Sports Commission says it recognises that "the cost of specialised equipment, travel, training and everyday living expenses" can be a barrier for Para athletes.

It also said investment by the federal government, through the Para Uplift program, has been extended for another two years, with the aim to "identify the critical issues affecting [athletes'] ability to enter, progress and succeed in high-performance sport".

Media and 'Cripspiration'

While media coverage of the Paralympics has vastly improved since the London 2012 Games, broader coverage of Para and disabled sport is still limited.

One of Australia's most celebrated Paralympians, Ellie Cole, is now a successful sports commentator and presenter. (Getty: Carmen Mandato)

In the survey, Ayers expressed that women get "hardly any free-to-air time or prime time coverage … and para-athletes [get] hardly any coverage, less than women."

Another respondent wrote that a lack of media coverage impacted sponsorship opportunities, saying: "It's extremely difficult to financially support yourself as an athlete across Olympic and Paralympic sports unless you are the greatest of all time or have an incredible story to sell."

Di Torro said it seemed like there was only room for one Para athlete at a time when it came to media focus and coverage.

"It's like you've either got the one fast person with one leg, or you've got the one great athlete who pushes a wheelchair really, really fast," she said.

There's also concern about the way Para athlete stories are being told.

Hannah Macdougall is an elite Para triathlete and dual Paralympian. (Supplied)

Para triathlete Dr Hannah MacDougall, who has also won Paralympic medals for swimming, researched issues around Para athlete sponsorship and media representation in her university Honours thesis.

MacDougall said non-disabled athletes were often associated with strength and power, whereas disabled athletes were seen as inspirational for overcoming their impairment.

The disability community has termed this narrative "cripspiration" and regards it as patronising.

"Media and imagery are so powerful; it's [2026], and we still get 'cripspiration'," MacDougall said.

"I have all of these strengths that often get overlooked because people see the two wheels [of the wheelchair] and they straight away go to pity."

Di Toro felt too many stories could be "clickbait", with the narrative focused on how the person acquired their disability, instead of placing their role as a high-performance athlete first.

"We [need to] start looking at the actual performances of people and start praising those things, rather than this kind of trauma-based stuff when they were at the worst point of their life," Di Toro said.

For Ayers, it was about ensuring marginalised communities like disabled people could see themselves represented.

Nikki Ayers has faced many different forms of discrimination in sport. (ABC News: Scott Jewell)

"When there's a person with a disability, male or female or queer, there's the pride and the worthiness that you feel, that we are worthy and that we are valued in society," Ayers said.

"It is why I think it's so important to be getting us out there in mainstream media so other members of the public can see that and see that there are people with disabilities doing what they love and achieving greatness as well."

Looking ahead

ABC's Elite Athletes in Australian Women's Sport survey is not alone in shedding light on the issues that disabled women athletes have experienced.

Griffith University's initial research into the experiences of disabled women, girls, and non-binary people in sport and physical activity has also revealed issues around funding, health and social attitudes.

Many respondents in the Griffith University research described instances of sexism and devaluing based on their gender.

One such respondent spoke about bullying and verbal abuse they had experienced, and like Ayers, were told they were not good enough.

"All of these factors are abuse and no swimmer in Australian culture should ever need to go through this," the respondent said.

What all this research does is pull back the covers on what is often not spoken about in sport, particularly for disabled girls and women.

The ABC Elite Athletes in Australian Women's Sport survey uncovered several barriers in sport that uniquely impact disabled girls and women. (Getty: Matthew Stockman)

Ultimately, Di Toro, Ayers, and MacDougall want to see disabled women and girls able to thrive in elite sport.

"You need women in leadership roles who have an impairment, who have a disability, have that seat at the table," MacDougall said.

For Ayers, who was now looking to compete at the Los Angeles Games in a new sport, it was fundamentally about feeling safe and empowered to fully be yourself in sport.

She wanted people to realise the impact discrimination could have, so we stop it from happening.

"The most frustrating aspect of dealing with discrimination in sport is there's very little change," she said.

"We should be able to just rock up as human beings that love a sport and want to wear the green and gold and win a gold medal for Australia. That's what it should come down to."

This story is part of the ABC Elite Athletes in Australian Women's Sport Survey.

World.title: 'Hurt ourselves': Wallabies survive scare as Kiss era begins with Japan win
World.content:
Wallabies coach Les Kiss says his side will need to learn how to control their ambitions after Australia won a frantic Test match over Japan in Osaka on Saturday night.

REPORT: Australia 35 defeats Japan 32 in Osaka

Japan threatened to earn a historic first Test win over Australia, taking an early lead and playing 20 minutes against 14 men after Wallabies lock Miles Amatosero was red-carded for a dangerous clean-out in the first half.

But the Wallabies were able to put together enough moments of class to win the high-tempo Test match in hot and humid conditions at the Hanazono Rugby Stadium.

The men in gold showed that when they play with polish, they are one of the best attacking sides in international rugby. But that polish was few and far between on Saturday night, allowing the Brave Blossoms to threaten the upset.

After winning his first match in charge since the departure of Joe Schmidt, Kiss said he was to get a positive result but improvement was needed ahead of next week's second Test in Townsville.

"[Japan are] a good team. They play fast and hard, and at home in their own backyard, they're a tough team to play against," Kiss told Stan Sport.

"[We] probably offered a few too many opportunities for them. Some kicking went astray [and we] overplayed a couple of times.

"You want to be able to be ambitious, while at the same time temper that.

"Overall, that's a Test win. Well done boys."

Japan came into the contest having never beaten Australia, but were in good form after beating Italy and showing promise against Ireland and France last month in the Nations Championship.

Victory for Australia means they have won consecutive Test matches for the first time in 12 months, after belting Italy in Perth last month.

Wallabies coach Les Kiss (left) and captain Harry Wilson (right) both say Australia has plenty to improve on. (Getty Images: Paul Miller)

Wallabies captain Harry Wilson said the team was "really happy" to win, but said discipline in both attack and defence was going to be a big focus at training in preparation for the second Test.

"I think we hurt ourselves way too much, but when we held onto the ball [and] went through them, I thought we looked really good too," he said.

"We pushed the pass too often. In these conditions, the ball is soaked, and we probably needed to be a bit smarter with it.

"In defence, sometimes we were a bit lazy. A few passive tackles and they get quick ball, and then they really put you under the pump."

Relive all the action from the Wallabies' first Test against Japan in the blog below.

World.title: Souths hang on to deny Eels remarkable comeback
World.content:
South Sydney concedes 24 unanswered second-half points but manage to hold on for a 28-24 victory, which consolidates the Rabbitohs' place in the league's top eight.

On a day of incredible NRL fightbacks, the Eels almost delivered the biggest of all time after trailing 28-0 at the break.

Earlier the Dolphins came from 24-0 down to beat the Broncos 40-32 in a remarkable Battle of Brisbane, while the Melbourne Storm came back from 14-0 down to hammer Manly Warringah 42-20 in Perth.

In Sydney though, the Eels looked as far from mounting a fight back as any team could be after a dire first half.

Alex Johnston's hat-trick, coupled with tries to Tevita Tatola, Brandon Smith and Jye Gray had Souths well on top at the Sydney Football Stadium.

Souths lost halfback Ashton Ward to a hamstring injury just before the break, while the Eels had Isaiah Iongi carried off with a knee injury in a brutal match played at an incredible pace.

But after the break, the Eels turned their form around dramatically, Tallyn Da Silva, Ryley Smith and Ronald Volkman scoring three tries in the space of six minutes to open the second stanza.

Jordan Samrani scored too, setting up a remarkable finale.

However, a magical 40:20 from Cody Walker with just over a minute on the clock secured the victory for Souths.

"It's just one of those ones that came off," Walker told Fox Sports after the match.

"I'm just happy with the two points, we needed that.

"We had players playing everywhere, we lost our halfback in the first half so we just had to win that and we did it.

"I'm pretty proud of the boys' effort."

Sea Eagles 'not good enough'

Sualauvi Fa'alogo helped ignite the Storm after they trailed 14-0 in the first half in Perth. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Earlier, the Sea Eagles lamented a horror performance that all but eliminated them from finals contention, needing to win their last four games to have a legitimate chance of making the top eight.

Manly coach Kieran Foran questioned his team's hardness and apologised to the club's fans after shipping 42-straight points in East Perth.

The Storm were horrible early in Saturday's match, with their completion rate sitting at just five of 12 as the Sea Eagles scored the opening two tries to race out to a 14-0 lead.

But it was all one way traffic from that point on, with Melbourne piling on six unanswered tries either side of half-time to turn the contest on its head.

"We can't explain it. I just don't feel that there's a real hard edge about our approach to our footy at the moment," Foran said.

"You know, 14-0 up, you should be in control of that game of footy. You should be able to put the foot on the throat and maintain a level of control.

"I feel very, very sorry to our fans.

"We had a lot to play for today. There was a lot on the line.

"There was good reason to turn up and put in a really good performance. And after about the half an hour mark, that just wasn't good enough.

"I had a bit to say [to the players] just before, but I'll keep most of it in house."

The Storm snapped a three-game losing streak, but at 9-12 they need to win their remaining three games and rely on other results to go their way in order to sneak into the post-season.

Dolphins bite back to beat Broncos

BRISBANE, AUSTRALIA - AUGUST 08: Connelly Lemuelu of the Dolphins is congratulated by team mates after scoring a try during the round 23 NRL match between Dolphins and Brisbane Broncos at Suncorp Stadium, on August 08, 2026, in Brisbane, Australia. (Photo by Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

The Dolphins produced arguably an even greater fight back in front of over 50m,000 supporters at Lang Park.

The Broncos tore out of the blocks in the derby, racing into a 24-0 lead early on, only to see the Dolphins flip the script with a remarkable second half display.

Tabuai-Fidow won the Battle Medal as man of the match, scored his second try in the 68th minute with stunning leap above Reece Walsh from a Katoa bomb to give the Dolphins a 36-32 lead, the first time they had hit the front.

"It's obviously a special round for myself, being a proud Torres Strait Islander," he said.

"So to get the win in this [Indigenous] round and especially against the Broncos, it's something special."

The Broncos, already out of finals contention, lamented the familiar defensive errors that have cost them the chance to defend their premiership crown this season.

"We just need to be better around our defence," coach Michael Maguire said.

"We all need to take ownership. Are we capable of being better than where we are? I believe so, definitely."

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: Why broadcasting row has Tour de France Femmes fans 'pissed off'
World.content:
The catchcry of the Tour de France Femmes by its lead sponsor, Zwift, is pretty simple: Watch the Femmes.

By and large, the viewership data shows that people are doing exactly that.

And why wouldn't they?

After a riveting seven days of racing so far, capped by Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney's masterful ascent of the legendary Mont Ventoux, the top three riders in this year's race are separated by just 39 seconds.

Six different riders have claimed stage victories so far, with the overall race lead changing hands three times since the opening stage.

The 2024 champion, Niewiadoma-Phinney, holds a 15-second advantage over Demi Vollering, the woman she beat two years ago by a measly four seconds.

This is a race that has had it all.

The three-way battle between Demi Vollering, Marlen Reusser and Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney has captivated fans this year. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

But fans, as yet, cannot watch the race in its entirety, with just three of the nine stages of this year's race televised from start to finish.

The lack of comprehensive live coverage is a growing pain that the women's edition of the Tour de France is hoping to overcome as the fifth edition of its most recent iteration comes to a close in Nice this weekend.

It is something that women's riders' union, The Cyclists' Alliance (TCA) — whose president is Australian former world and Olympic champion Grace Brown — has criticised throughout the race.

"For the biggest race in women's cycling, partial coverage is no longer enough," TCA wrote in a social media post.

The 'accursed' mountain that stands apart this Tour de France The ascent to hell on the punishing slopes of Mont Ventoux is one of the Tour de France's most formidable and iconic theatres.

"Fans will still miss the attacks, the tactics, and the moments that could define the race."

Broadcaster Orla Chennaoui, who hosts the coverage for TNT Sports in the UK, was less diplomatic.

"I'm getting really annoyed now. I'm getting really, really pissed off," she said on an Instagram reel that she titled: Women's sport done a disservice Editions #4957.

"What the heck? There is so much excitement and interest in the Tour de France Femmes.

"The riders, the race have proven over and over again how dynamic and dramatic this sport is.

"I have never seen my [social media] algorithm so flooded with excitement, with joy, with celebration for this race.

Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney won her first Tour de France Femmes stage on the slopes of Mont Ventoux. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"It's everywhere, on Instagram, podcasts popping up all over the place, YouTube videos, more written articles that I would ever have imagined when I started covering women's cycling 10 years ago.

"And we still, despite this, despite how proven the interest is, we cannot get live TV coverage.

"ASO [Amaury Sport Organisation], what are you doing? Why can we not get to watch all stages live?"

The astonishing story behind the women's Tour The Tour de France Femmes produced one of the closest finishes in cycling stage race history last year. But when the women's Tour was first revived, it was called "ugly".

Chennaoui said there was a "huge will" from broadcasters to show the race in its entirety every day in that post, which she acknowledged she may get in trouble for and be asked to delete.

All 21 stages of the men's Tour de France were broadcast live in their entirety.

On the same day that the third stage of the women's Tour de France Femme was half-shown, stage one of the men's Tour de Pologne World Tour race was shown in full, all five hours, four minutes and 11 seconds of what was a flat, 234.2-kilometre race.

The duration of the Tour de France Femmes broadcast has increased to 27 hours and 40 minutes for this year's race, up five hours and 20 minutes from what was shown live in 2024.

However, TCA noted that France Télévisions data showed a 40 per cent increase in viewership from 18.3 million in 2024 to 25.7 million in 2025.

"The demand is undeniable," TCA said.

"We are asking for the coverage to catch up."

One of the pre-race favourites, Demi Vollering crashed early in the stage. (Getty Images: Alex Broadway)

That post was put up in the hours before stage three took place, a stage won by Norway's Sigrid Haugset with an 88km breakaway attack.

However, the move that saw the Norwegian break away from the peloton was completely missed, as the TV cameras had not started rolling.

Additionally, one of the pre-race favourites, Vollering crashed early in the stage, an incident that was, again, missed by the cameras, and could have huge repercussions for the rest of the race.

"That was disappointing," former world champion on the track and the road Lizzie Deignan told the For The Love Of Cycling podcast.

"There's no substitute for footage. You can't get a feel of the race, of the tension, of the atmosphere."

According to organisers, this year's Tour de France Femmes is being broadcast in 190 countries, including by SBS in Australia.

France Télévisions keeps the supporters of women's cycling in the shade with their coverage. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Romain Doucelin)

However, SBS and the Tour's other broadcast partners around the world can only show the footage they are provided with.

France Télévisions handles production and distribution of the broadcast on behalf of the Amaury Sport Organisation [ASO].

The ASO is also responsible for the men's Tour de France, as well as other major cycling events, including two of cycling's monument one day races, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Paris-Roubaix.

The organisation was heavily criticised for its coverage of the women's edition of Paris-Roubaix earlier this year, with less than 90 minutes of the three-and-a-half hour race shown.

"Paris-Roubaix this year, regardless of what they are going to say about TV numbers, was a step backwards," Chennaoui said in her Instagram reel.

"They're still doing a disservice to women's racing."

Tour de France Femmes race director Marion Rousse says things are moving in the right direction. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

As for the Tour de France Femmes, Deignan, who won the 2020 edition of La Course by Le Tour de France, a one-day precursor to the current women's multi-stage Tour, said the lack of coverage was a return to the "old days" of following professional cycling.

"It was very hard to follow from home," Deignan said of stage three of this year's Tour.

"It was like being back in the old days, refreshing news feeds, trying to figure out what's going on."

Cycling Weekly spoke to race director Marion Rousse about the criticism, and she said the race was moving towards full broadcast coverage.

"We're giving serious consideration to broadcasting all the stages in full in the future because the women deserve it," Rousse told Cycling Weekly.

"It works well in terms of audience figures.

"We're currently giving it real consideration, which is a step forward. Things are moving in the right direction."

World.title: Crows get home after almighty Tigers scare in the wet
World.content:
After the ugliest of wins, Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks and his players had a collective wry grin.

"There were some smiles at the end, when you actually realise you get four points for that performance," he said.

Nicks acknowledged Adelaide's slogging nine-point victory over cellar dwellers Richmond — 9.9 (63) to 7.12 (54) — was ugly.

"If you play that way and win, maybe it's a good sign," he said after the rain-marred Adelaide Oval fixture.

"That even when we're nowhere near our best — and that was ugly tonight, unfortunately — and yet we still got the job done.

"There will be some guys that are challenged out of this one. And we'll learn from that and get better."

The Crows will simply have to be better to make any inroads in their upcoming finals campaign, let alone their next task: taking on ladder-leaders Fremantle in Perth on Friday night.

"We have got a short break into Freo," Nicks said.

"And there will be some changes to our side, everything going well."

Adelaide forward Darcy Fogarty has served his three-game suspension and first-choice ruckman Lachlan McAndrew will return from a rest.

Key defender James Borlase will be available after a hamstring scare and utility Luke Nankervis should return from a chest injury.

But the fifth-placed Crows, on 56 premiership points, blew a chance for a significant win that would have taken fourth spot from Brisbane — they trail the Lions by 0.2 per cent.

Nicks rejected any suggestion his team suffered from an attitude problem against the 17th-placed Tigers.

"It's not an attitude, it's never an attitude thing — that is not out group," he said.

"People have got it a little bit wrong: the competition is not that uneven.

"There are talented players on every team in the comp.

"There are some that have got a little more experience than others, and and a little bit more talent here and there.

"It was always going to be a tough game."

Port Adelaide star Jason Horne-Francis gave his team a big injury scare when he limped off in the final quarter against Sydney. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

Meanwhile, Jason Horne-Francis hobbled off the field in Port's 97-point loss to Sydney, as Geelong made light work of Essendon, triumphing by 67 points at Kardinia Park.

Earlier on Saturday, a huge final quarter from Harrison Petty helped Melbourne claim a four-point win over the AFL's ladder-leaders Fremantle.

Petty kicked 3.2 for the afternoon, including two in the final quarter as Melbourne emerged 17.11 (113) to 17.7 (109) winners in one of the games of the season at the MCG.

Prior to the action on Saturday, AFL boss Andrew Dillon addressed Geelong's concussion saga, ending a couple of days of silence from the league.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: AFL chair apologises for his part in Cats concussion contract saga
World.content:
AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond has apologised for his part in Geelong's controversial concussion contract with defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

Drummond was Geelong president two years ago when premiership defender Kolodjashnij signed a contract in which he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

It is understood Kolodjashnij's agent was not aware of the contract, and neither the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) or AFL were informed at the time.

It is also understood that while Kolodjashnij passed an independent medical test, he was still considered at risk of future complications from head injuries.

Jake's twin brother, Kade, was forced to retire from the game in 2020 due to ongoing concussion problems.

"I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024," Drummond said.

"This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board.

"Jake's welfare was central to all discussions, and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days.

Cats face 'please explain' Geelong is finally issued a 'please explain' over its controversial concussion contract with premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

"While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play.

"Regardless of the player's agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed."

Drummond said it was an error to keep the process quiet, and clarified that he would not be involved in AFL discussions about the matter.

"As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA," Drummond said.

"I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations.

"I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation."

Speaking to ABC Sport ahead of the Saturday games, AFL boss Andrew Dillon reiterated that it was a complex situation.

"This is an issue that is really complex and in this one in particular it's complex and unique," Dillon said.

"But concussion and the effects that has on players or participants in contact sports ... is an issue that's confronting contact sports worldwide.

"What we have here is a player that has suffered multiple concussions, went before an AFL concussion panel, ultimately over a period of months was cleared as fit to play.

"Through that period, over a number of months, Jake's worked with the club doctors, independent medical experts, the club, and the club board and management to make sure that he understood their were risks to continue playing, not withstanding that you've been cleared medically fit to play.

"That was the intent behind what was going on."

Dillon said the please explain was around why the concussion agreement sat alongside his playing contract.

"We've gone to Geelong under the rules and asked them why it wasn't lodged with us," Dillon said.

"So we're waiting to hear back from Geelong on that."

The Cats are expected to be fined over the contract saga after initially being cleared of wrongdoing.

World.title: Surprise parents' visit inspires new leader in Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney launched a decisive attack up Mont Ventoux to win the seventh stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the overall lead from Marlen Reusser.

The 2024 champion was in tears as she put on the yellow jersey and now leads 2023 champion Demi Vollering by 15 seconds and Reusser by 39 with two stages left.

"I'm just so tired and so blown away with what just happened," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"When I started climbing I looked to the right and I saw my parents standing on the roadside. They came today by surprise. I saw my father yelling for me and I thought I had to make him proud."

Reusser and Vollering could not follow Niewiadoma-Phinney when she broke away about 9km from the top of Ventoux, one of the most iconic climbs in cycling with its barren, lunar aspect.

It was a first Tour stage win for Niewiadoma-Phinney, who won the 2024 edition without claiming a stage. Gritting her teeth in the final few hundred metres, the Polish rider dug deep and with the sun gleaming behind her, raised her arms after crossing the line.

She then almost lost balance through fatigue and had to be helped off her bike. Moments later, she was all smiles as she sat on the road and poured cooling water over her head.

"I never chase victories for the sake of winning, I target them because I like this beautiful feeling I have right now," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"I came here (before) to Mont Ventoux with my friends and my husband, and we rode up the climb three times.

"The feeling of reaching the top of this mountain was amazing. From that moment, I just wanted to experience that feeling again. The pure joy of riding, as if I was a kid."

Vollering dropped Reusser in the closing stages of the 15.7km ascent of Ventoux, which has featured several time on the men's Tour. In one of the darkest days in Tour history, British rider Tom Simpson died after collapsing during a tortuous ascent in 1967.

World time trial champion Reusser battled gamely but lost valuable time in the title fight. The Swiss rider finished the stage fourth as Vollering and two-time Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy both placed ahead of her.

There were three smaller climbs heading to Ventoux, which was ranked as a Hors Catégorie ascent — the hardest category — and had a gradient of nearly 9 per cent.

Vollering moved ahead first, and Reusser and Niewiadoma-Phinney joined her as others lagged behind. Niewiadoma-Phinney then attacked and, although Vollering stood up in her saddle to chase her the new race leader was riding a brilliant tempo and proved too strong.

"My idea was that I had to make it to Chalet Reynard on my own," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"Because from then on the headwind would be quite strong and the chasers would try to stay on each other's wheel for as long as possible."

The eighth stage is a flat 172km route for sprinters finishing in Nice, where the race ends after another mountain stage on Sunday night.

Stage nine features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, nestled in the hills overlooking the Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on the final stage to win the race by just four seconds.

Tech.title: X replaces its revenue-sharing program with ‘Original Content Rewards’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

X is ending its controversial revenue-sharing program for content creators, which has seen numerous revisions under Elon Musk’s reign. In its place, it’s launching a new Original Content Rewards program on September 8th. To be eligible, creators must have at least 500 verified followers and at least 500,000 Home Timeline impressions from verified users in the last 90 days, among other requirements.

Creators will then earn revenue based on “qualified impressions” on “original content.”Qualified impressions are unique impressions from Premium subscribers “on the Home Timeline feed, where at least 50% of the post is visible.” What qualifies as “original content” exactly? Well, that’s a little harder to define. Under the guidelines, original reporting or analysis, videos and photos taken by the user, as well as graphics or illustrations made by the creator, including memes. X also says that commentary or reactions still qualify, as long as they “add something meaningful.”

In the post announcing the program, the company says the goal is to shift the focus away from exploiting loopholes and clickbait. Simply repurposing content from others or replying to posts wouldn’t be a viable source of income under the new system, theoretically. Allegra Jacchia, Senior Product Manager, Creators at SpaceXAI, said on X that the program was designed to “reward the creators who bring original ideas, expertise, creativity, and unique perspectives to 𝕏 -- not those who have become best at gaming the system.”

Participants in the revenue-sharing model will continue to earn revenue through September 7th.

Tech.title: An Amazon data center could have the worst polluting power plant in the country
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

To power its new West Texas data center, Amazon is investing in the construction of a new power plant that could be one of the largest single producers of greenhouse gases in the US, according to the New York Times. The new gas-burning plant in Pecos County, Texas has received significant investment from Amazon and, at least initially, would not be connected to the state’s power grid. Instead, its 35 natural-gas turbines would primarily deliver its 7.65 gigawatts of electricity to the new data center.

According to Cleanview, which tracks data centers and their associated power projects, GW Ranch received a permit from Texas allowing for the emission of up to 33 million tons of CO2, more than even the largest coal plant in the country. Plants rarely emit as much greenhouse gas as their permits allow, but it’s still notable that the restrictions on its pollution levels are so lax. Amazon has confirmed that it purchased the site and plans to purchase power from GW Ranch.

Even if the GW Ranch site only emits a portion of the greenhouse gases it’s permitted to, it would still represent a significant setback for Amazon’s Climate Pledge. Jeff Bezos pledged to make his company carbon neutral by 2040. However, its emissions have climbed for several years in a row due to the demands of AI. Amazon spokeswoman Margaret Callahan told the New York Times that, “The world looks different now than when we co-founded the climate pledge,” but that, “our commitment hasn’t changed.”

Tech.title: Buc-ee’s dodges John Oliver to sue another small business
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Buc-ee’s became something of a viral sensation during the World Cup, but it has a troubling history of suing small gas stations and convenience stores. On a recent episode of Last Week Tonight, John Oliver literally begged the company to sue him for selling merch featuring his squirrel mascot, Mr. Nutterbutter, with branding that reads “Buc-Off.” But Buc-ee’s has so far declined to take the bait, instead targeting yet another small business that lacks the deep pockets and legal team of HBO.

According to WDTN, an NBC affiliate in Miami Valley, Ohio, Buc-ee’s opened its first locations in the state earlier this year. And now it’s targeting established local businesses through trademark suits. Beaver’s Mini Mart in Beavercreek has been a staple of the city for “decades.” But Buc-ee’s is claiming that this long-running store’s beaver logo could confuse customers. WDTN says:

In the suit, filed days ago, Buc-ee’s alleges that the Mini Mart’s cartoon beaver mascot is too similar to their own, with its “wide eyes and a smile” that also “uses red as a predominant color,” and could cause confusion.

Oliver and Mr. Nutterbutter have already fended off one lawsuit, with Bob Murray, a mining executive, having unsuccessfully sued for defamation following a 2017 episode about the coal industry.

Tech.title: Musician and entrepreneur Tom Vek is building a digital music player, but don’t call it retro
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Tom Vek burst onto the scene in 2005 with his album We Have Sound, which garnered a solid 7.6 from the tastemakers of the day over at Pitchfork. His undeniably catchy brand of dancy indietronica landed him an appearance on The OC and placement on the Grand Theft Auto IV soundtrack. His follow-up, Leisure Seizure, had a lengthy gestation period, but arrived in 2011 to similar success, reaching No. 79 on the UK charts.

Vek has continued to release music at regular intervals over the last 15 years, dropping Newer Symbols in 2022. But in 2020 he started toying with this idea he had for a music player called Sleevenote. Inspired by vinyl packaging, it was his way of trying to bring some of the beauty and magic of cover art and liner notes to your digital audio. Securing parts, like square screens, proved difficult. Plus, the original prototype was enormous — roughly the size of a 7-inch single, just thicker and heavier.

Now Vek is back with a new version of Sleevenote that’s smaller, cheaper, and, for a little while longer, available to purchase. The last handful of the Day One Editions are available now for $349. As he turns his attention to the next chapter for his media player passion project, he told us about the essentials, his obsessions, and pet peeves as a musician-turned-entrepreneur.

What is your most indispensable tool (analog or digital, app or hardware)?

As much as I’d love to say my GMT wristwatch, because of all the communication we do with our friends in Seattle, and my love of wristwatches, the real answer has to be a MacBook. I’m either designing UI, designing graphics, retouching photos, or making videos, discussing ideas, implementing ideas, or hearing how my ideas go down. It truly is the motorbike for my mind. I have to see ideas to know whether I like them or not. I’m very fickle regarding industrial design of the tech I use and a big fan of the current “M” MacBooks, Apple kinda lost it for a bit.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

I get a lot of shit from Sleevenote co-founder Chris for how many tabs I have open, also in multiple Chrome profiles, you know, to the point the tabs get so narrow that you have to remember what it is from the favicon. I like coming back to things, as well as having a selection of regularly used things in a row. I find it useful for remembering all the social apps I’m meant to be posting my latest Sleevenote graphic to.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

This is a bit salty, but the trend for new retro-style CD players and cassette players. It is a great sign that people want offline dedicated music experiences, but I want to see new ideas. I’m specifically interested in ideas that push for digital music purchasing because it’s far better for musicians than buying that second-hand CD. I want my kids’ generation not to be stuck in a retro cycle, or a doomed big tech cycle. I want to see thoughtfully created indie tech products that could not have existed at any other time. Plus, I remember cassettes, they sound awful.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

I will answer this with a song: three years after my debut album, when I should have had my second album together, I heard “Jump In The Pool” by Friendly Fires, featuring one of the most stunning synth solos of all time. I would have loved to have created that song at that time. Especially since I’d pushed myself and my then manager fully-clothed into a pool around that time and hadn’t even thought to write a song about it.

What is your current obsession?

Been an obsession for quite a while but it’s still: carports in architecture. I’m a car guy, I’m a very visually-focused car guy. I’m not really fussed about performance or track racing or anything. My real love is the design of the automobile and how it’s an emotive expression of movement. The perfect abode to me has car(s) on show, not hidden away in a garage, but still protected, so the carport becomes this perfect idea. I’m obsessed with mid-century desert architecture which incorporated the automobile so well into the language of the house, but even in the rainy UK, being able to get in and out of your car without getting wet would just make me so happy, I think haha.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

I buy lots of fiction books. I love a small paperback. I just picked up a book called The Cowards based purely on the cover. I’ve just finished a load of Steinbeck, so looking for something else. It’s funny that I often use the shortest elevator pitch “Sleevenote is a Kindle for music”, but I’ve never liked the idea of a digital book. Most people read one book at a time, but having all your music accessible at any one time is much more of a reason for a digitisation of a collection, it seems to me.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Digital music downloads are worth splurging on. We’ve been led to believe there’s no point in buying anything digitally, but it’s standing in plain sight as the best thing to do with things like music. Not only does it send far greater support for artists, but it gives us music fans offline and time-stamped access to great art, and being encouraged to spend some time with a curated selection of art, we all know is good for the mind and soul. I want Sleevenote to enable this.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Encompassing all my work, I suspect it would be “Nothing But Green Lights”, the name of one of my songs, which I’d also apply to my work with other projects. It’s good, not always easy, to try to think there’s nothing in the way of going where you want to go.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: Is this $450 laptop from an unknown brand too good to be true?
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Finding a good laptop under $500 was hard enough before RAMageddon. They nearly always had cheap hardware and underpowered, often outdated chips. That’s what made the MacBook Neo so disruptive: It offered great build quality and good-enough performance starting at $599. Windows laptops couldn’t touch it. Even though it’s gone up to $699, it’s still the laptop to beat.

So when little-known Chinese brand Chuwi announced a $450 Windows laptop with an aluminum build and a brand-new Intel Wildcat Lake processor, it sounded too good to be true.

It is.

3 Verge Score Chuwi UniBook $ 449 $ 449 The Good It’s $450

Tons of ports for a small laptop (though none are very fast)

Good battery life The Bad A bad screen and absolutely awful trackpad, speakers, and webcam

Metal chassis feels cheap, with lots of flex

Lackluster performance from the Intel chip and limited RAM

Concerns over long-term customer support $449 at Chuwi How we rate and review products

The UniBook comes in one configuration: a 14-inch with an Intel Core 3 304 processor, 8GB of soldered RAM, and a user-swappable 256GB SSD. That’s the lowest-end of Intel’s new Wildcat Lake chips, with just five CPU cores: one performance core, and four low-power efficiency cores. And the integrated graphics? A single GPU core. The MacBook Neo’s A18 Pro is a six-core CPU / five-core GPU ensemble, and it’s a hot rod by comparison.

Component report card Screen: D

Webcam: D

Keyboard: C

Trackpad: F

Port selection: A

Speakers: F

Number of ugly stickers to remove: 1

The UniBook feels sluggish in anything beyond basic web browsing, emails, and messaging. Its benchmark scores confirm how woefully underpowered that chip is. The MacBook Neo trounces it across the board: both single and multicore CPU performance, as well as graphics. Our Adobe Premiere 4K export test took over an hour on the UniBook. (Although at least it didn’t crash out.) I know it isn’t designed for video editing, but neither is the MacBook Neo, and the Neo exports the same video in under 10 minutes. The one edge the UniBook has is a slightly faster SSD.

Chuwi UniBook / Intel Core 3 304 “Wildcat Lake” / 8GB / 256GB MacBook Neo / Apple A18 Pro / 8GB / 256GB Microsoft Surface Laptop 13-inch (2026) / Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus X1P-46-100 / 8GB / 256GB Acer Aspire 14 AI / Intel Core Ultra 7 256V “Lunar Lake” / 16GB / 1TB Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x / Qualcomm Snapdragon X X1-26-100 / 16GB / 256GB CPU cores 5 6 8 8 8 GPU Intel Graphics (1 GPU core) A18 Pro (5 GPU cores) Adreno X1-45 Intel Arc 140V (8 GPU cores) Adreno X1-26 Geekbench 6 CPU Single 2385 3402 2348 2769 2137 Geekbench 6 CPU Multi 6187 8508 9421 10930 9728 Geekbench 6 GPU (OpenCL) 6019 19798 9554 28556 9689 Premiere 4K Export (lower is better) 1 hour, 9 minutes, 29 seconds 8 minutes, 30 seconds Crashed 7 minutes, 28 seconds 12 minutes, 59 seconds Sustained SSD reads (MB/s) 2394.57 1735.91 3804.31 6391.51 5738.86 Sustained SSD writes (MB/s) 2092.66 1684.05 3310.94 5524.22 2801.02 Price as tested $449 $699 $949.99 $1,049.99 $749.99

But despite faster storage, the UniBook’s 8GB of RAM is still a hindrance on Windows 11. It didn’t randomly lag like the recent 13-inch Surface Laptop did, but it isn’t hard to overwhelm. As on the 8GB Surface, Windows 11 uses anywhere from 4.6 to over 5GB of memory on the UniBook after a fresh reboot with no additional apps running. Once you open a half dozen Chrome tabs, a couple messaging apps, and a music streaming app, memory usage easily climbs to 7GB.

It’s no surprise Chrome crashed on me a couple times when I pushed it further with over 20 tabs across multiple virtual desktops. This is no problem on Windows laptops with 16GB of RAM, and even the MacBook Neo could handle more before slowing down. And you can count on everything moving like molasses during big file transfers. It couldn’t even load the Start menu or open the calculator app while importing photos into Lightroom Classic until the RAM and SSD bottlenecks eased.

Simple looks. Frustrating use.

Even if your computing needs are minimal, the Chuwi’s hardware makes every interaction unpleasant. The screen is washed out, covering just 64 percent of the sRGB color space, and at 300 nits it’s pretty dim. But the worst offender is the trackpad. It’s incredibly stiff to click. You have to press it so hard the whole chassis flexes a little under the pressure. You don’t have to click the trackpad; it can detect taps too, but I never like the loosey-goosey feel of tapping — especially when executing right-clicks or click-and-drags. Using this trackpad made me physically and mentally tired. And clicking around on a laptop? Pretty important!

The speakers are an affront to any music you play, as well as anyone else within earshot. They’re a tinny mess. The phone in your pocket has fuller sound. The 720p webcam is only a smidge better, but it’s still offensive to your face (and possibly your self-confidence). It’s almost passable in the best lighting, but it’s low-res, with a green color cast. In dim or backlit lighting you become a dark blur. After a few days, colleagues started greeting me in meetings with, “Oh, you must be on the Chuwi.” It’s like being told “Wow, you look tired.”

“Uhh, yeah. Nice to see you too.”

Look at all these ports. Dang. Now if only they were fast. A cromulent keyboard.

Amid all these downsides, there are a few bright spots. The UniBook does at least have good battery life. It easily lasts up to 10 hours on battery while doing the lightest of work: writing emails, casually browsing the web, and opening the occasional PDF. And the keyboard isn’t bad. It’s backlit, which is a genuine advantage over the MacBook Neo. It’s fine to type on, but the Neo’s and many other Windows keyboards out there feel less spongy. Also, a lack of function lock means adjusting brightness, volume, or media playback always requires a two-key combo. Not a huge deal, but a strange omission of a usual mainstay.

The one thing about the UniBook that genuinely surprised me, aside from the initial reverse sticker shock, was its amount of ports. This little thing has five total USB ports, HDMI-out, microSD, and even an ethernet jack. You might expect all that on a massive gaming laptop, not a thin-and-light. But sadly, none of the USBs are faster than 5Gbps, and the HDMI is just 1.4b — topping out at a stuttery 30Hz at 4K.

Any money spent on peripherals to offset the Chuwi’s shortcomings would be better spent on a different laptop. I’ve started testing a $500-ish HP OmniBook 3, and coming from the Chuwi, it was a huge relief. Even its cheap-as-they-get Snapdragon X chip offers eight cores, buoyed by twice the RAM and storage of the Chuwi, and that processor already proved it had exceptional battery life when I reviewed it in the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x.

Previous Next



1 / 3 I despise this trackpad.

I wasn’t overly impressed with the Acer Aspire 14 AI, which you can often get around $600, when I pitted it and the IdeaPad against the MacBook Neo, but it’s way better than the Chuwi for $155 more. Its Intel Lunar Lake chip gets good battery life and is powerful enough to play indie games and last-gen 3D titles on ultra-low settings. It has twice the RAM and storage as the Chuwi and nearly as many ports, and the Acer’s ports are much faster.

I take no joy in telling you the Chuwi UniBook is bad and frustrating to use. I want to see decent cheap laptops, and I’m all for them coming from lesser-known brands. But Chuwi’s upstart status also brings long-term customer support into question — it doesn’t seem to have US customer service and repair centers like bigger laptop makers. And in early 2026, the company was found to have shipped laptops and mini PCs with older AMD chips disguised as newer, faster ones (even at the BIOS level). Chuwi eventually put out a statement blaming a “production error” and offered refunds for a limited time, but the situation does not inspire confidence.

It’s a shame the UniBook is uniformly bad.

The UniBook doesn’t leave a great first impression, but I want to remain hopeful that better things are on the horizon — if not for Chuwi, then at least for the Wildcat Lake processor family. Most of the major laptop makers are launching budget laptops with higher-end Wildcat Lake chips to try to compete with the Neo. Microsoft also claims it’s working on improving Windows 11’s performance with 8GB of RAM — which these new laptops desperately need.

With laptop prices skyrocketing due to the RAM and storage crunch, we could all use a win. But the UniBook isn’t it.

They’ve also built a couple of really cool productivity-adjacent apps, including Kerouac (which is basically like that GitHub commit chart but for writing) and recently Post Through It, which is basically a journaling app that looks like a private Twitter. Clever!

Anyway, I asked JA to share their homescreen to see if they might have other sneaky tips up their sleeve, or more awesome apps to show. Here it is, plus some info on the apps they use and why:

The phone: I use an iPhone 17 Pro Max, 512GB.

The wallpaper: My wallpaper is Mors Imperator (“Death Is the Ruler”), by the German artist Hermione von Preuschen. It’s on display in Berlin right now and I fell in love with it on a recent trip. The apps: Insight Timer, Beeper, Spotify, Pocket Casts, Buffer, Cursor, 1Password, Replit, Termius, Granola, Kilo, Kerouac, Post Through It, Buzz, Wikipedia, Marvel Unlimited, Linear, Medium, GenZD, The New York Times, Obsidian, Vimcal, Readwise Reader, Kobo.

My home screen is a mix of reading, working, playing etc. I definitely want to call out Kerouac (a writing studio for pro bloggers) and Post Through It (microblogging for one) which are PWAs of the apps I launched this year. I’m a big believer in web apps as a way to avoid app store gatekeeping, so I’m on a mission to make the PWAs of my own tools as top-notch as they can be, which means using them every day myself.

I keep the Kobo app in my dock so I push myself to read an actual book instead of doomscrolling; and I don’t keep any social media apps installed. If I want to post, I have Buffer on my home screen, and it’s connected to my Hermes agent via MCP anyway. I use Beeper to manage my chats across Discord, Slack, Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, etc; it’s a fantastic tool that probably rescues me from chat hell a thousand times a day.

GenZD and Marvel Unlimited are my favorites. The first is a GZDoom client for playing Doom 1 and Doom 2, Heretic, Hexen, and their mods (3D shooters from the ’90s). The other is Marvel’s digital comics app, where I’m attempting to read every Spider-Man story since the inception of the character. Other than that, it’s work, note-taking and podcasts.

I also asked JA to share a few things they’re into right now. Here’s what they sent back:

I have rediscovered my love for MC Lars . He’s a “nerdcore” indie rapper who came to fame with songs about Edgar Allan Poe, Shakespeare etc. He’s been a favorite of mine for years, but I introduced my kid to his music this year, and he’s been in constant rotation since. “I Was Never Afraid” is his all time best song.

The Paradox are the best band I’ve heard in a decade. They play pop punk the way it should be played, with so much energy and joy I can’t not jump out of my seat when I hear it. I recommend their track “ Good For Me ,” which I think is going to be on their new EP in October.

I’ve been reading Barbarians at the Gate: the Fall of RJR Nabisco , by Bryan Burrough and John Helyar. A wild story of leveraged buyouts, Wall Street excess, and the unhinged market economics of the 1980s. An absolute page turner, even if you’re not usually interested in the subject matter.

My brother has started us on a Daggerheart campaign. It’s a tabletop RPG that came out last year, with a heavy emphasis on storytelling, and it’s the freshest take on roleplaying I’ve experienced in a while. Really makes you want to get inside the character you’re running and think about who they are — which is a great exercise for me as a writer.

I’m about to go on parental leave, which previously in my life has been a good time to change stuff on my phone. I delete all the work apps, turn off some notifications, all that stuff. But you know what’s really making me do it this time? The Google Health app. I haven’t been wearing my Fitbit Air recently — no good reason, just haven’t been finding it useful — and every single day the app sends me a sad notification that’s like, “Oh no, I haven’t collected any data, pretty please let’s get the Fitbit back on?” No thanks, I hate it.

Anyway, I’ve also been noticing that some of the smartest people I know are always showing that they “have notifications silenced” in iMessage. So I’m learning from them, and turning everything off. From now on, my phone will have no buzzing or noise-making notifications other than phone calls. I’ll see things when I decide to check my phone… which hopefully won’t be very often. Silent phones forever!

Tech.title: Nitecore’s latest power bank is the lightest and most compact yet
Tech.content:
is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

There’s two things you should know about me, your intrepid reviewer: I hate the feature creep associated with modern power banks, and I love shaving grams off the gear I carry when backpacking, bikepacking, and trail running. So imagine my delight when Nitecore released a new generation of its ultralight NB10000 battery. After a few weeks with it I can confidently say: Haribo be damned!

The $83.95 NB10000 Gen 4 weighs just 146 grams, according to my scale, and measures 1.45 x 11.6 x 4.68cm (0.57 x 4.57 x 1.84 inches), according to Nitecore’s spec sheet. That makes it the lightest and most compact 10,000mAh power bank I can find. Even when factoring in the extra 6 grams added by the included USB-C lanyard, it still beats the previous ultralight champ: Nitecore’s NB10000 Gen 3. The secret to the Gen 4’s impressive weight is a silicon-carbon anode, the same battery tech increasingly appearing in flagship smartphones, including Samsung’s.

As small as it is, the Gen 4’s 39Wh battery still fully recharged my aging iPhone 15 Pro twice, with a few watt-hours left in the tank. And with up to 22.5W of output, it can even top-up my 14-inch MacBook Pro when needed. It also supports pass-through to charge your gadgets as the power bank itself charges.

Have I found power bank perfection? Almost.

I like that the NB10000 Gen 4 gets all the basics right. It has a simple, four-element indicator to show the battery level, which I much prefer over a fancy display. It’s constructed out of carbon fiber sheets and offers IPX7 protection against water ingress, allowing it to withstand rain or even temporary submersion – exactly what you want from an adventure battery.

In my testing, I measured 33.58Wh of the claimed 39Wh capacity for an 86.1 percent efficiency. That’s a pretty good result for a premium power bank and a slight improvement on the 33.33Wh we measured on the Gen 3 model. That works out to 229.98Wh/kg of delivered energy, or 220.90Wh/kg with the cable — class-leading results, either way. The NB10000 Gen 4 supports PD, QC3.0, and Huawei’s SCP charging protocols.

The Gen 4 battery on top of an iPhone 15 Pro. It’s very small for the charge capacity it holds. The RGB lights are pretty but a little superfluous and that button is touch-sensitive instead of mechanical. Silly. Carbon fiber shell with strong IPX7 resistance to water ingress. Supports pass-through charging to charge and be charged simultaneously.

The Gen 4 model also didn’t suffer from the overheating and shutdown issues we saw when the Gen 3 would run low on juice. I did, however, see a temporary interruption in power delivery when the Gen 4 unit was almost fully depleted, but that’s only because I had a meter attached — otherwise I wouldn’t have known since it continued charging almost immediately.

The only thing that could be considered superfluous is the animated RGB lighting that flows around the dual USB-C ports. The lights are there to guide you to the USB-C ports in a dark tent, says Nitecore, but you can also… feel them. Give the battery a double-knock near the top and the lights (and battery indicator) illuminate. This can be helpful if wearing gloves since Nitecore inexplicably opted for a touch-sensitive wake button on the Gen 4. Fortunately, that so-called “Touch Button” did reliably sense my wet finger in testing. The knock-to-wake feature seemed to only work about 75 percent of the time, but it, and the RGB lights, can be disabled if you want.

Previous Next













1 / 8 The lanyard is actually a braided USB-C cable rated for up to 60W.

The lights will also glow yellow (regular mode) or green (eco) after a long press of the power button if you want to toggle between full power and extended life, respectively. Eco mode works by dropping the output to a slow 5W (5V at 1A) max. This can keep the power bank from automatically shutting off when charging low-draw devices like headlamps, watches, or wireless earbuds. It can also yield a little more total charge capacity by producing less heat waste, and allow the battery to operate closer to its native voltage resulting in less conversion loss.

The Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 is the ideal power bank for endurance athletes, backpackers, or anyone looking for an ultralight and ultracompact power bank that mostly avoids feature creep. The only real negative is the price, having gone up to $83.95 since the launch of the $64.95 Gen 3 model two years ago. That makes the Gen 4 power bank two to three times more expensive than the typical 10,000mAh power bank, but it can save you 50 grams or more. That’s a price premium I can see lots of active, outdoorsy people happily paying for.

Tech.title: The gaming site sponsored by Walmart lays off its editorial staff
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Restart, a games media website launched in late 2024 that was sponsored by Walmart, has laid off its “entire editorial team,” according to a Friday post from Brandy Berthelson, the site’s former editor-in-chief. Other staffers have also posted about being laid off.

Restart is operated by Moonrock, a content marketing agency, though its editorial mission page says it’s “powered” by Walmart. That page outlines how Walmart is (or was) involved:

When we mention a game, we’ll provide purchase links that will take you to Walmart using a partner tracking code. This link provides us with 0% of the sale if you decide to buy the product, but it does help Walmart see exactly how customers arrived at the product.According to that page, Restart operated as an “independent site” and said that Walmart “doesn’t influence our editorial direction.”

According to that page, Restart operated as an “independent site” and said that Walmart “doesn’t influence our editorial direction.”

Basically, Restart was Walmart’s take on something like Game Informer, which used to be owned by GameStop. A few months before the launch of Restart, GameStop shut Game Informer down, though it’s since been revived under new ownership.

Berthelson says she is “not able” to discuss details of the layoffs. One laid off staffer tells The Verge that they signed a severance agreement with Moonrock.

As of this writing, Restart remains online. It’s unclear if Walmart and Moonrock will continue operating the site following the layoffs, and if so, what that will look like. Walmart and Moonrock didn’t immediately reply to requests for comment.

Tech.title: Planned Amazon data center could become the biggest climate polluter in the U.S.
Tech.content:
In Brief

As part of a planned data center in Pecos County, Texas, Amazon is investing in an on-site power plant that could become the largest source of climate pollution in the United States, according to The New York Times.

The NYT says the plant would burn natural gas and is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year — more than any other power plant in the U.S.

In a statement, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the data center will “be powered by new on-site generation that won’t raise electricity costs for Texas families.” (Data centers face growing political opposition for a number of reasons, including their effect on electricity costs.)

AI has already had a significant impact on Amazon’s carbon emissions, which it reported were up 16% last year — the wrong direction for a company that pledged to eliminate its carbon emissions by 2040. And that could get worse as Amazon and tech companies back the development of huge natural gas plants to support their power-hungry data centers.

The Amazon spokesperson said, “The world looks different now than when we co-founded the climate pledge,” while also claiming, “Our commitment hasn’t changed.”

Tech.title: OpenAI acquires presentation startup NextSlide

The NextSlide website currently displays a note from founder Ahmed Beshry describing the startup’s product as one “that could turn prompts, notes, documents, or research into a polished, editable presentation.”

The ultimate goal, Beshry said, was “to make visual communication more accessible and help more people express their ideas clearly.” So by joining OpenAI, the team will “continue pursuing that same mission: building AI products that help people create, communicate, and turn their ideas into meaningful work.”
